arXiv:2611.14083v1 [cs.CR] 10 Nov 2026

Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument
for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models

Tomer Solberg Affiliation: MoonMath.ai Email: research@moonmath.ai
Abstract

We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} without any floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. Within one domain, the proof batches zerochecks and the leaf layer of LogUp-GKR lookups into a single sumcheck. Lookups are split into chunks of fewer than pp lookups, which LogUp needs for soundness in a prime field. Every witness tensor and weight lives in one multilinear commitment, built from a rate-1/21/2 Reed–Solomon code, BLAKE3 Merkle trees of mixed height, and a mixed-length BaseFold opening over the degree-8 extension. The prover streams the model layer by layer in two passes, recomputes the witness where it would otherwise store it, and runs on one GPU with a device-resident Fiat–Shamir transcript and CUDA-graph replay of identical layers. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for one sequence of 4,096 tokens, 253 s for four such sequences, and 398 s for one sequence of 16,384 tokens. The same prover covers Qwen3-32B, which adds QK-norm, and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B, proving 4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s. A proof takes 41 to 50 times as long as computing the same tokens in our serving engine for F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}, or 6.4 cents for a 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. The price of exactness is accuracy: on WikiText-2, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}’s greedy token matches the BF16 model’s at 86.3% of positions and its perplexity is 8.3% higher; we trace about a third of this gap to the 8-bit queries and keys. On Qwen3, choosing per key-value group how the score exponent is split between queries and keys, which costs nothing in the proof, removes 53% of the perplexity gap of Qwen3-30B-A3B and 23% of that of Qwen3-32B, and on both models F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. We reduce the work of the verifier, which a recursive compression must arithmetize, from 17.817.8 to 4.24.2 million BLAKE3 compressions for a 4,096-token proof of the full model, and a verifier with a compiled core checks the proofs of all three models on one CPU core in 1919 to 5656 s. We also give a BLAKE3 circuit in the same proof system, whose constraint proof costs 2.8​μ2.8\,\mus per compression. In the random-oracle model and with proven proximity bounds, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2−1032^{-103}, counting a 30-bit proof of work on the queries. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system as built is meant for open-weight models and for verifiers, such as auditors, that can afford a proof of 106 to 477 MiB. The prover, the verifier and the scripts behind every measurement are available under the MIT license at https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable.

1 Introduction

A client that sends a prompt to a hosted language model receives text and nothing else. It cannot tell which model produced the text, whether the weights were quantized more aggressively than advertised, whether the answer was cut short, or whether the sampling decisions were made with the randomness it was promised. Verifiable inference asks the server to attach evidence that the output yy equals F⁡(W,x,r)F(W,x,r) for the prompt xx, a sampling seed rr the server did not choose, and weights WW fixed by a public commitment CWC_{W}. The evidence can come from trusted hardware, from re-execution by other parties, from statistical fingerprints of the computation, or from a cryptographic proof. Only the last gives a guarantee that rests on cryptographic assumptions alone and can be checked by anyone, at any later time, without the weights.

Cryptographic proofs of neural network inference have so far been costly. Systems based on sumcheck and GKR proved convolutional networks [LXZ21] and later language models with up to 1313 billion parameters in under fifteen minutes per inference [SLZ24]. Circuit-based systems compile models into general-purpose SNARKs [CWSK24, Zko23]. Three obstacles separate these results from proving the inference that a server actually performs on a production-size model.

The function must be exact.

A proof establishes a relation between integers or field elements. Floating-point inference is not a function of its inputs in that sense: results change with the kernel, the batch shape and the order of reductions [HT25], and a single changed argmax or sampling decision changes every later token. A proof system therefore needs a precisely defined integer function FF, and the server must serve that function. Approximate checks of the floating-point computation, as in [OFP+25], answer a different question.

The constraints must not wrap.

Small prime fields make provers fast, since a base-field element fits a machine word and arithmetic needs no multi-precision code [Pol24, HLP24, BDT24]. They also make every intermediate quantity of a transformer large compared to pp: a dot product of 2152^{15} products of 8-bit integers reaches 2292^{29}, and a softmax denominator over 2202^{20} keys reaches 2302^{30}, against p≈231p\approx 2^{31}. A relation that holds modulo pp but not over the integers lets a prover change the computation and still pass. Every relation must therefore be accompanied by bounds that keep both sides below pp.

The proof must scale.

For one 16,384-token sequence through Qwen2.5-32B, the trace has about 6×10116\times 10^{11} committed field elements and 7×10117\times 10^{11} lookups. This trace does not fit in GPU memory or in host memory, and the number of lookups exceeds pp, so the multiset argument of LogUp [Hab22] is unsound unless the lookups are partitioned.

1.1 Contributions

  • •

    An exact integer transformer (Section 5). We define F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}, an integer function for Qwen2-style decoder-only transformers, and extend it to the QK-norm and mixture-of-experts layers of Qwen3. Activations are 24-bit, matrix products take 8-bit inputs with power-of-two scales placed off the reduction axis, and attention and the MLP use fused rounding steps. Sampling, greedy or by inverse CDF, reads a seed derived from a client nonce. A deterministic program maps a BF16 checkpoint to F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}.

  • •

    A wrap-free constraint system over a 31-bit field (Section 6). Every gadget comes with integer bounds, under which the relation over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} is equivalent to the relation over ℤ\mathbb{Z} (Lemma 6.1). Every gadget also has exactly one satisfying output (Lemma 6.2). Range and table checks go through one tagged table of 2262^{26} rows.

  • •

    A streamed proof built from three primitives (Section 7). A domain proves the zerocheck and the leaf layer of the LogUp-GKR trees of a set of columns in one sumcheck (Lemma 7.1). Lookups are split into chunks of at most 2302^{30} lookups, each with its own multiplicity column, and one GKR over the table proves all chunks at once (Lemma 7.2). Claims flow backward from the output to the embedding, so the prover makes two passes over the model and never holds more than one layer’s witness. All tensors and weights live in one multilinear commitment whose openings are batched across sizes and whose Merkle paths are shared across the tensors of a layer.

  • •

    A single-GPU prover (Section 9). Sumcheck round kernels are generated per constraint program and run their first rounds on base-field tables. The Fiat–Shamir transcript runs on the GPU, one warp per BLAKE3 compression, so the prove pass has no host round trips. One middle layer’s prove pass is captured as a CUDA graph and replayed for the other layers. 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} products use one modular reduction per coordinate.

  • •

    A verifier that a recursion can afford (Section 10). Public columns are evaluated in closed form, fixed tables are committed, final openings are recorded without being hashed into the transcript, and tensors share columns and Merkle paths. Together these steps cut the verifier’s hashing by 4.2×4.2\times, and the proof for 4,096 tokens from 360360 to 134.8134.8 MiB. We also build the first component of the recursive circuit: BLAKE3 compressions as rows of a domain, with a LogUp memory that wires the rows together.

  • •

    Evaluation and analysis (Sections 8 and 11). We measure the prover on all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B and on Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, relate its time to the inference it attests and to prior systems, measure what exactness costs in accuracy and which integer steps cause the loss, and give a soundness analysis with every term of the error budget. The analysis of tuple compression in LogUp (Lemma 8.1) shows that compressing a tuple of arity kk with the powers of one challenge costs log2⁡k\log_{2}k bits, so Sable draws one challenge per tuple coordinate.

The implementation, its tests and the scripts that produce every measurement in this paper are released under the MIT license at https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable.

1.2 Scope

The main proof is not zero-knowledge: it reveals evaluations of the trace to its verifier. It is large, 134.8134.8 MiB for one 4,096-token sequence through the full model, and a verifier with a compiled core takes 1919 s on one CPU core to check it. As built, Sable therefore produces an auditor’s proof for open-weight models: a non-zero-knowledge proof that reopens the committed weights would leak closed weights after about 2×1042\times 10^{4} proofs. Section 4 states the threat model, the trust anchors of the verifier and these limits. A recursive layer that proves the verifier, with zero-knowledge outer layers, is the intended form for every client; Section 10 reports the parts of it that exist. The statement concerns F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} itself, and the BF16 checkpoint it was derived from plays no role in it, so the accuracy of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} relative to the original model is part of what a deployment must report (Section 11.8).

2 Related work

Proofs of machine-learning inference.

Early systems proved small networks with general-purpose SNARKs or with interactive proofs specialized to matrix products. zkCNN [LXZ21] introduced a sumcheck-based argument for convolutions, building on the GKR line of work. Mystique [WYX+21] used VOLE-based interactive zero-knowledge proofs with conversions between arithmetic and Boolean values. ZKML [CWSK24] and ezkl [Zko23] compile models to Halo2 circuits and optimize the circuit layout. For language models, zkLLM [SLZ24] combines sumcheck for tensor operations with a lookup argument (tlookup) for non-arithmetic operations and a dedicated protocol for attention; it proves models up to 13B parameters and outputs short proofs through a pairing-based commitment. zkGPT [QSL+25] targets GPT-2-sized models with optimized constraint layouts for non-linear functions and proves GPT-2 in about 22 s on a CPU. Section 11.4 compares proving times per parameter and token. zkLLM and zkGPT work over large prime fields (BLS12-381 or BN254 scalar fields), where a single field element holds any intermediate value, and both approximate non-linear functions without fixing the integer semantics of the served model. Sable differs in three respects: it works over a 31-bit field and pays for that with explicit no-wrap bounds; it defines the served function bit for bit, including normalization, softmax, sampling and stopping; and it targets models and contexts large enough that the trace must be streamed.

Concurrent work.

FlashProve [Ant26, RAC+26], a concurrent system from Anthropic, proves inference of Llama 4 Maverick, a mixture of experts with 400.7400.7B parameters of which a token uses 16.1516.15B, from a third-party 4-bit release of its weights. It replaces the model by an integer function with table-based non-linear steps, as we do, and compiles interactive oracle proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks field with Reed–Solomon codes, BLAKE2b Merkle trees and zero-knowledge proximity tests; the proof hides the weights, it is about 18.818.8 MB per request, and the soundness, completeness and zero knowledge of the protocol are proved in Lean, while its C++ and CUDA programs are tested. On one H100 it proves 1,024-token windows at about 111 tokens per second in batches of 24; under its default policy a proof checks one token, the greedy successor of the window, and an optional policy checks every token of a stored reply against a looser criterion than greedy choice. Sable differs in what it proves and where it is measured. A Sable proof covers a whole reply: every generated token, the stopping rule, and, at a positive temperature, sampling from a seed fixed by the statement, FlashProve does not check sampling, and a reply cut short verifies there as a shorter reply. Sable proves contexts of up to 16,384 tokens, where attention, quadratic in the length, is about half of the work, against 1,024 there. Our commitment to the weights is a plain Merkle root that anyone can recompute from an open checkpoint and that serves any number of proofs, while FlashProve’s hiding commitment bounds the number of batches it can serve, at most 688,127. We report the accuracy of the integer model on full task benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K) against BF16 and two deployed 8-bit schemes; FlashProve reports how often its greedy token differs from the 16-bit model’s on WikiText-2 (6.8%6.8\% and 9.4%9.4\% of positions on two text sets) and runs no task benchmark. Its prover needs about 260 GB of host memory, against at most 188 GB (175 GiB) for ours. Per active parameter and token, FlashProve’s mixture of experts takes about as long as Sable’s dense proofs and 6 to 11 times less than Sable’s proofs of Qwen3-30B-A3B (Section 11.4), with zero knowledge included and at a shorter context. FlashProve’s zero knowledge, proofs 6 to 27 times smaller than ours, faster proofs of a mixture of experts with about twelve times as many parameters as our models, and machine-checked protocol mark directions of future work for Sable: zero-knowledge and recursive layers that shrink the proof (Sections 10 and 12), proofs of larger mixtures of experts at a lower cost per active parameter, and a machine-checked proof of the protocol.

Other approaches to trustworthy inference.

Trusted execution environments on GPUs attest to the code that ran, under a hardware trust assumption. Refereed delegation [CRR11] and optimistic schemes resolve disputes by re-execution, which requires deterministic computation and an honest party with the weights. TOPLOC [OFP+25] hashes features of the floating-point activations so that a verifier with the model can check, approximately and statistically, that a claimed computation was performed. Our statement is exact and our verifier does not need the weights, at a much higher proving cost.

Sumcheck, GKR and lookups.

The sumcheck protocol [LFKN92] and the GKR protocol [GKR15] underlie provers whose cost is linear in the computation. Thaler [Tha13] gave linear-time provers for matrix products and regular circuits; Libra [XZZ+19] made GKR linear-time for general circuits and added zero knowledge; Spartan [Set20] and HyperPlonk [CBBZ23] built SNARKs for constraint systems around zerochecks over the Boolean hypercube. Lookup arguments started with Plookup [GW20]; LogUp [Hab22] replaced grand products by sums of logarithmic derivatives, and Papini and Haböck [PH23] proved those sums with GKR, which removes any commitment that depends on the lookup challenge. Lasso and Jolt [STW24, AST24] use structured tables and sumcheck-based lookups for virtual machines. Our domains combine the last GKR layer of all lookups with the zerocheck of the same columns in one sumcheck, and our chunking follows from the observation that LogUp only proves inclusion modulo the characteristic.

Small fields and sumcheck prover algorithms.

STARK provers moved from 64-bit fields to 31-bit fields (Mersenne-31, BabyBear, KoalaBear) for speed on CPUs and GPUs [Pol24, HLP24]; Binius [DP25] works over binary towers. In all of them, soundness needs challenges from an extension field. Gruen [Gru24] showed how to remove the equality factor from zerocheck round messages and how to skip the first round’s extension arithmetic. Bagad, Domb and Thaler [BDT24] and Dao et al. [DDB+26] gave sumcheck provers that keep most work in the base field when the summed polynomials take small values. Our prover evaluates the first round of every sumcheck on base-field tables and folds them into extension tables in the second round; the more aggressive small-value algorithms of [BDT24, DDB+26] would apply to our constraint programs only with extension-field coefficients, which Section 9.2 discusses.

Hash-based polynomial commitments.

FRI [BSBHR18a] tests proximity to Reed–Solomon codes and underlies STARKs [BSBHR18b]; its soundness up to the Johnson bound follows from the proximity gaps of Ben-Sasson et al. [BSCI+20], and Haböck [Hab24] analyzes BaseFold over Reed–Solomon codes in the same list-decoding regime. Multilinear commitments from linear codes include Ligero [AHIV17] and Brakedown [GLS+23]; BaseFold [ZCF24] folds a foldable code alongside a sumcheck, and WHIR [ACFY25] reduces the verifier’s queries. Our commitment uses BaseFold over Reed–Solomon codes on multiplicative subgroups, batches columns of different lengths by joining them at the matching fold level, as in batched FRI for mixed degrees, and arranges all columns of a layer under one Merkle tree whose height differs per column size.

GPU provers.

GPU acceleration of proof systems has concentrated on multi-scalar multiplication and number-theoretic transforms for pairing-based SNARKs [MXS+23, LWY+23] and on STARK provers over small fields (for example sppark and ICICLE). Sable’s kernels are generated per constraint program and per field, and its transcript runs on the GPU, so that the whole prove pass of a layer can be replayed as one CUDA graph.

Integer inference and quantization.

Integer-only inference fixes the arithmetic of a network so that it runs on integer units [JKC+18, KGY+21]. LLM.int8() [DLBZ22], SmoothQuant [XLS+23], QuaRot [AMC+24] and SpinQuant [LZF+25] quantize transformers to 8 bits or fewer by handling activation outliers, through mixed precision, scale migration or rotations. F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} uses a random orthogonal rotation fused into the weights in the manner of QuaRot, per-row dynamic exponents for activations, and per-column exponents for weights, and it replaces every floating-point non-linearity with a table.

Recursion.

Incrementally verifiable computation [Val08] and recursive SNARKs compress long proofs by proving their verifier. Hash-based recursion that evaluates the hash inside the circuit is standard for STARKs and is usually paired with an algebraic hash; we keep BLAKE3 everywhere, which makes the recursion circuit larger and avoids a further hash assumption.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Notation and fields

For an integer nn, [n]={0,…,n−1}[n]=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}. An index i∈[2n]i\in[2^{n}] is identified with its bit vector (i0,…,in−1)∈{0,1}n(i_{0},\ldots,i_{n-1})\in\{0,1\}^{n}, i=∑j2j​iji=\sum_{j}2^{j}i_{j}, so coordinate jj of a point is bit jj of the index (little-endian). A=[−223,223)A=[-2^{23},2^{23}) is the activation range. ⌊⋅⌉\lfloor\cdot\rceil denotes rounding half up, ⌊z+1/2⌋\lfloor z+1/2\rfloor.

Throughout, p=231−224+1p=2^{31}-2^{24}+1 (KoalaBear), so p−1=224⋅127p-1=2^{24}\cdot 127 and 𝔽p×\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times} contains a cyclic subgroup of order 2k2^{k} for every k≤24k\leq 24. We use the tower

𝔽p2=𝔽p​[x]/(x2−3),𝔽p4=𝔽p2​[y]/(y2−x),𝔽p8=𝔽p4​[z]/(z2−y),\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}=\mathbb{F}_{p}[x]/(x^{2}-3),\qquad\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}}[y]/(y^{2}-x),\qquad\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}=\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}[z]/(z^{2}-y),

so that 𝔽p4≅𝔽p​[Y]/(Y4−3)\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}[Y]/(Y^{4}-3) and 𝔽p8≅𝔽p​[X]/(X8−3)\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}\cong\mathbb{F}_{p}[X]/(X^{8}-3). These are fields: p≡2(mod3)p\equiv 2\pmod{3} and p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4}, so by quadratic reciprocity 33 is a non-residue modulo pp, and a binomial X2k−aX^{2^{k}}-a with aa a non-residue is irreducible over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} when p≡1(mod4)p\equiv 1\pmod{4} [LN97, Thm. 3.75]. |𝔽p4|≈2124|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|\approx 2^{124} and |𝔽p8|≈2248|\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}|\approx 2^{248}. Witness values lie in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}; interactive-proof challenges lie in 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} and commitment challenges in 𝔽p8⊃𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}\supset\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}.

3.2 Multilinear extensions

The multilinear extension of f:{0,1}n→𝔽f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\mathbb{F} is the unique multilinear f~:𝔽n→𝔽\widetilde{f}:\mathbb{F}^{n}\to\mathbb{F} that agrees with ff on {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}:

f~​(r)=∑x∈{0,1}neq⁡(r,x)​f​(x),eq⁡(r,x)=∏j=0n−1(rj​xj+(1−rj)​(1−xj)).\widetilde{f}(r)=\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}\mathrm{eq}(r,x)\,f(x),\qquad\mathrm{eq}(r,x)=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\big(r_{j}x_{j}+(1-r_{j})(1-x_{j})\big).

A vector of length 2n2^{n} is a function on {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} through the index convention above. We write f~​(r)\widetilde{f}(r) for the evaluation of a vector at rr and call a pair (r,v)(r,v) with claimed v=f~​(r)v=\widetilde{f}(r) a claim on ff. For a matrix M∈𝔽2a×2bM\in\mathbb{F}^{2^{a}\times 2^{b}} stored row-major, M~​(rc,rr)\widetilde{M}(r_{c},r_{r}) takes the column variables first.

3.3 Sumcheck and zerocheck

Lemma 3.1 (Sumcheck [LFKN92]).

Let g:𝔽n→𝔽g:\mathbb{F}^{n}\to\mathbb{F} have degree at most dd in each variable. In the sumcheck protocol for ∑x∈{0,1}ng⁡(x)=c\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{n}}g(x)=c, the prover sends in round jj a univariate polynomial of degree at most dd, the verifier checks it against the running claim and replies with a random rj∈𝔽r_{j}\in\mathbb{F}, and at the end the claim is reduced to g⁡(r)=vg(r)=v. If ∑xg⁡(x)≠c\sum_{x}g(x)\neq c, the verifier accepts a false final claim with probability at most n​d/|𝔽|nd/|\mathbb{F}|, and at most d/|𝔽|d/|\mathbb{F}| per round.

All our sumchecks have the form ∑xw⁡(x)​∑tct​∏k∈tTk​(x)\sum_{x}w(x)\sum_{t}c_{t}\prod_{k\in t}T_{k}(x) for multilinear tables TkT_{k}, coefficients ctc_{t} and either w=1w=1 or w=eq⁡(r,⋅)w=\mathrm{eq}(r,\cdot). Products of tables are formed as polynomials in table values, so a constraint of degree dd in the columns gives a sumcheck of degree dd (plus one for eq\mathrm{eq}). In the eq\mathrm{eq} case the prover sends the round polynomial without the eq\mathrm{eq} factor of the round variable, as in [Gru24], which lowers its degree by one.

A zerocheck proves that a polynomial expression C⁡(f1​(x),…,fm​(x))C(f_{1}(x),\ldots,f_{m}(x)) in committed vectors vanishes on {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n}. It runs the sumcheck for ∑xeq⁡(τ,x)​C​(x)=0\sum_{x}\mathrm{eq}(\tau,x)C(x)=0 for a random τ\tau. If C⁡(x∗)≠0C(x^{*})\neq 0 for some x∗x^{*}, the multilinear extension of x↦C⁡(x)x\mapsto C(x) is a nonzero multilinear polynomial, which vanishes at a random τ\tau with probability at most n/|𝔽|n/|\mathbb{F}|.

A product sumcheck reduces a claim on a matrix product C=A​BC=AB, C~​(rx,ry)=v\widetilde{C}(r_{x},r_{y})=v, to the sumcheck ∑kA~​(rx,k)​B~​(k,ry)=v\sum_{k}\widetilde{A}(r_{x},k)\,\widetilde{B}(k,r_{y})=v, whose prover costs O⁡(m​k+k​n)O(mk+kn) field operations after folding AA and BB at rxr_{x} and ryr_{y} [Tha13].

3.4 Fractional sums and LogUp

Lemma 3.2 (LogUp [Hab22], over a prime field).

Let a1,…,aN∈𝔽a_{1},\ldots,a_{N}\in\mathbb{F} with N<pN<p, let T⊂𝔽T\subset\mathbb{F} be a set, and let m:T→𝔽m:T\to\mathbb{F} be arbitrary. If the rational functions

∑i=1N1Z−aiand∑v∈Tm⁡(v)Z−v\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{Z-a_{i}}\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{v\in T}\frac{m(v)}{Z-v}

in 𝔽⁡(Z)\mathbb{F}(Z) are equal, then every ai∈Ta_{i}\in T, and m⁡(v)m(v) equals |{i:ai=v}||\{i:a_{i}=v\}| modulo pp.

The bound N<pN<p is needed: pp copies of a value a∉Ta\notin T contribute p/(Z−a)=0p/(Z-a)=0. No bound on the multiplicities is needed, which is why they may be committed as arbitrary field elements. LogUp tests the identity at a random ZZ. A tuple (u0,…,uk−1)(u_{0},\ldots,u_{k-1}) is compressed to the single value u0+β1​u1+⋯+βk−1​uk−1u_{0}+\beta_{1}u_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{k-1}u_{k-1} for independent random βi\beta_{i}, which we collect as β=(β1,…,β8)\beta=(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{8}); Lemma 8.1 bounds the error of the combined test. Following [PH23], the sums are evaluated by a binary tree of fractions: the leaves are (ni,qi)=(1,Z−ai)(n_{i},q_{i})=(1,Z-a_{i}), and a parent is

(n,q)=(n0​q1+n1​q0,q0​q1),(n,q)=(n_{0}q_{1}+n_{1}q_{0},\ q_{0}q_{1}),

so the root is a fraction (P,Q)(P,Q) with P/QP/Q equal to the sum. GKR proves the tree layer by layer: a claim on the multilinear extensions of layer kk at a point becomes, by one sumcheck of degree 3, a claim on layer k+1k+1 at a new point. No committed value depends on ZZ, so every column, including the multiplicities, is committed before ZZ is drawn.

3.5 Codes, commitments and Fiat–Shamir

Let Hk⊂𝔽p×H_{k}\subset\mathbb{F}_{p}^{\times} be the subgroup of order 2k2^{k}. The Reed–Solomon code RS⁡[k]\mathrm{RS}[k] of rate 1/21/2 encodes a message m∈𝔽p2k−1m\in\mathbb{F}_{p}^{2^{k-1}}, read as the coefficients of f⁡(X)=∑jmj​Xjf(X)=\sum_{j}m_{j}X^{j}, as the evaluations of ff on HkH_{k}. Positions are in bit-reversed order, so the two symbols f⁡(ω),f⁡(−ω)f(\omega),f(-\omega) are adjacent, and the four symbols that reduce to one symbol after two folds are contiguous. Folding with a challenge rr maps the pair (a,b)=(f⁡(ω),f⁡(−ω))(a,b)=(f(\omega),f(-\omega)) to

a+b2+r⁡(a−b2​ω−a+b2),\tfrac{a+b}{2}+r\Big(\tfrac{a-b}{2\omega}-\tfrac{a+b}{2}\Big),

which is the encoding in RS⁡[k−1]\mathrm{RS}[k-1] of the folded message (1−r)​meven+r​modd(1-r)m_{\mathrm{even}}+r\,m_{\mathrm{odd}}. The folded message is the restriction of the message’s multilinear extension to x0=rx_{0}=r, so a sequence of folds with challenges r0,r1,…r_{0},r_{1},\ldots ends in the constant m~​(r)\widetilde{m}(r). BaseFold [ZCF24] interleaves these folds with a sumcheck of eq⁡(ρ,x)​m~​(x)\mathrm{eq}(\rho,x)\,\widetilde{m}(x) to prove m~​(ρ)=v\widetilde{m}(\rho)=v. Its soundness reduces to the proximity of the committed oracles to the code, which FRI-style queries test; in the unique-decoding and Johnson regimes the error is bounded by the proximity gaps of Ben-Sasson et al. [BSCI+20].

Merkle trees are built with BLAKE3 [OANWO20]; a tree’s cap is the list of its 272^{7} nodes at depth 77, sent in place of the root, and paths stop at the cap. The protocol is made non-interactive with the Fiat–Shamir transform [FS86]. The transcript absorbs every prover message, prefixed with its length in bytes, and derives each challenge from its state, by rejection sampling of 31-bit words into 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} coordinates; after a challenge it absorbs a separator and the first 32 output bytes. Its hash is the BLAKE3 compression function 𝖢⁡(h,m,t,ℓ,f)\mathsf{C}(h,m,t,\ell,f) (chaining value hh, 64-byte block mm, counter tt, block length ℓ\ell, flags ff) in a sequential mode of our own, which is not a standardized BLAKE3 mode. The state is a chaining value hh, initially the BLAKE3 IV, and a pending block. When a block is full and more input arrives, h←𝖢⁡(h,mt,t,64,0)h\leftarrow\mathsf{C}(h,m_{t},t,64,0) for the tt-th block. Output block jj is 𝖢⁡(h,m,j,ℓ,chunk_end∣root)\mathsf{C}(h,m,j,\ell,\textsc{chunk\_end}\mid\textsc{root}) on the pending block mm of length ℓ≤64\ell\leq 64, which is never empty unless nothing was absorbed. This is a Merkle–Damgård iteration whose final call carries the length of the last block and flags that no absorbing call uses, so the encoding of the absorbed string is prefix-free and absorbing and output calls are separated. With the compression function modeled as ideal, as in BLAKE3’s own analysis, such an iteration is indifferentiable from a random oracle [CDMP05], and the Fiat–Shamir analysis below applies to it unchanged. Compared with BLAKE3’s tree mode, which derives every output from the root of a tree over 1,024-byte chunks, a challenge costs one compression instead of one per level of the tree; this matters because a proof draws about a million challenges, each on the prover’s critical path and each to be arithmetized by a recursive verifier. For interactive oracle proofs [BSCS16] with round-by-round soundness error ϵ\epsilon [CCH+19], the resulting argument has soundness error at most Q​ϵQ\epsilon against provers that make QQ random-oracle queries, up to the collision probability of the hash. We report security in bits as log2⁡(1/ϵ)\log_{2}(1/\epsilon), the convention used for deployed STARKs.

3.6 Verifiable inference

Definition 3.3 (Statement and relation).

A statement is a tuple 𝗌𝗍=(CW,𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗒,x,y,nc)\mathsf{st}=(C_{W},\mathsf{policy},x,y,n_{c}): a weight commitment, a decoding policy (temperature index θ\theta, maximum output length GmaxG_{\max}, stop tokens), a prompt x∈VPx\in V^{P}, generated tokens y∈VGy\in V^{G}, and a client nonce nc∈{0,1}256n_{c}\in\{0,1\}^{256}. The seed is r=𝖲𝖧𝖠𝟤𝟧𝟨⁡(seed​‖nc‖​CW​‖𝖲𝖧𝖠𝟤𝟧𝟨⁡(x)‖​𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗒)r=\mathsf{SHA256}(\texttt{seed}\,\|\,n_{c}\,\|\,C_{W}\,\|\,\mathsf{SHA256}(x)\,\|\,\mathsf{policy}). CWC_{W}, the seed and the digests of the statement (Section 7.6) use SHA-256. The main verifier evaluates SHA-256 over the caps of the weight units (for CWC_{W}) and over the model’s constants and tables (for hcirch_{\mathrm{circ}}); a recursive verifier would take those caps and constants as public inputs, so that their SHA-256 digests are checked outside the circuit. The relation ℛ\mathcal{R} contains (𝗌𝗍,W)(\mathsf{st},W) exactly when CWC_{W} is a commitment to WW, yy is the autoregressive output of F𝖮​(W,⋅,r)F_{\mathsf{O}}(W,\cdot,r) from xx (yty_{t} is sampled from the logits at position P+t−1P+t-1 of x|y<tx\|y_{<t}), and yy obeys the stopping rule: no yty_{t} with t<Gt<G is a stop token, and either yGy_{G} is one or G=GmaxG=G_{\max}.

Because F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is deterministic and causal, all S=P+G−1S=P+G-1 positions can be evaluated in one teacher-forced pass over xx followed by the first G−1G-1 generated tokens (the last generated token is output but never read), and the logits at each generated position equal those of a token-by-token decode. The prover therefore proves one forward pass over SS positions together with the sampling decisions at the last GG positions.

Definition 3.4 (Batched statement).

A batched statement (CW,𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗒,(xb,yb)b<B,nc)(C_{W},\mathsf{policy},(x_{b},y_{b})_{b<B},n_{c}) has BB prompts of equal length and generated sequences of equal length GG, one policy and one nonce. Its seed is r=𝖲𝖧𝖠𝟤𝟧𝟨⁡(seed​‖nc‖​CW​‖𝖲𝖧𝖠𝟤𝟧𝟨⁡(x0​‖⋯‖​xB−1)‖​𝗉𝗈𝗅𝗂𝖼𝗒)r=\mathsf{SHA256}(\texttt{seed}\,\|\,n_{c}\,\|\,C_{W}\,\|\,\mathsf{SHA256}(x_{0}\|\cdots\|x_{B-1})\,\|\,\mathsf{policy}), and sequence bb samples its token tt with ub,t=PRF⁡(r,b​G+t)u_{b,t}=\mathrm{PRF}(r,bG+t). ℛ\mathcal{R} contains (𝗌𝗍,W)(\mathsf{st},W) when every (xb,yb)(x_{b},y_{b}) satisfies the conditions of Definition 3.3 with these sampling values.

The verifier of a batched statement needs every xbx_{b} and yby_{b}, and the proof opens values of every sequence’s trace, so a batch is either one client’s sequences or is verified by a party entitled to see all of them.

An argument for ℛ\mathcal{R} is sound if no efficient prover makes the verifier accept a statement outside the language of ℛ\mathcal{R}, except with small probability. The stopping rule is part of the relation because otherwise every prefix of a valid output would also be valid, and a server could truncate answers.

4 Threat Model and Scope

Adversary and trust anchors.

The adversary is the server, which runs the prover and wants a verifier to accept an output that is not F𝖮​(W,x,r)F_{\mathsf{O}}(W,x,r) for the committed WW. The verifier trusts three things. (i) A registry that publishes, with the model release, CWC_{W} and a digest hcirch_{\mathrm{circ}} of every constant outside the weights (exponents, shifts, biases, tables and the commitment digests of the fixed tables). For an open-weight model anyone recomputes both from the checkpoint and the published quantization program, so the registry needs no trust beyond that recomputation. The server must never be the source of either, since a server that supplies hcirch_{\mathrm{circ}} chooses the tables. (ii) Its own tokenization: the statement is over token ids, so the client tokenizes and must receive the full sequence, including any system prompt the server prepends; a proof over a sequence with a hidden prefix proves a different statement and is rejected. (iii) Its nonce ncn_{c}, which fixes the sampling seed.

Who verifies.

The proof is not zero-knowledge, it is 106 to 477 MiB long for the three models we evaluate, and our verifier takes 19 to 56 s on one CPU core (Section 11.7). As built, it is therefore an auditor’s proof: the verifier is a client or an auditor that can afford this, for a model whose weights are public. A recursive proof of the verifier with zero-knowledge outer layers is the intended form for every client, and Section 10 reports its first components.

Open weights.

The proof reveals the trace at the queried positions, and the weights are committed once and reopened by every proof. Each proof opens every weight column at 153 random leaves of four Reed–Solomon symbols, and a column of 2232^{23} values is determined by any 2232^{23} of its 2242^{24} codeword symbols. After TT proofs, a client holds an expected fraction 1−e−153T/2221-e^{-153T/2^{22}} of the leaves, so about 222​ln⁡2/153≈1.9×1042^{22}\ln 2/153\approx 1.9\times 10^{4} proofs suffice to recover every weight by linear algebra. A provider that served a closed model with this prover would therefore publish it. The system as built is for open-weight models; closed weights need a hiding weight commitment, which the planned zero-knowledge layers provide. The soundness theorem also assumes that CWC_{W} commits to in-range weights (|w|≤127|w|\leq 127, Section 8). For open weights this is checked by recomputing CWC_{W}; for closed weights, a one-time range proof per model release would replace the assumption.

Batches.

A batched proof, such as our 4×44\times 4K shape, proves that each of several sequences is an output of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} under one CWC_{W}, one policy and one nonce, with the seed derived from all prompts (Definition 3.4). Its verifier needs all prompts and outputs and sees opened values of every sequence’s residual stream. A batch is therefore either one client’s sequences or is verified by an auditor entitled to see all of them; batching the requests of different clients would leak their prompts to each other.

Refusals.

A server can always decline to answer, and two kinds of refusal deserve mention. First, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is a partial function: on inputs where an intermediate value leaves its range, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is undefined and the honest prover aborts (Section 5.7). For open weights the client can evaluate F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} itself and confirm such an abort; Section 11.9 measures how often one occurs. Second, at temperature θ>0\theta>0 a server could refuse requests until a client’s fresh nonce yields a seed it likes. Clients can defend against this by counting refusals per prompt, or by sending nonces only under a commitment that obliges the server to answer. At θ=0\theta=0 the proof is a deterministic function of the statement and the nonce plays no role, so a server may cache and replay the proof of a repeated prompt, which is harmless.

Verifier cost under attack.

The verifier checks the statement, the policy, and the weight and fixed-table commitments against the registry before it replays the transcript, and it checks the 11-bit and 30-bit proofs of work when it reaches them, so a malformed proof fails early. A proof that fails only at its last query still costs a full verification.

5 The integer function F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}

F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is defined for decoder-only transformers in the style of Qwen2: pre-normalization with RMSNorm, grouped-query attention with biases on the query, key and value projections, rotary position embeddings (RoPE) [SAL+24], and a gated MLP with SiLU. Our running example is Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct [YYZ+24]: L=64L=64 layers, width d=5120d=5120, MLP width dff=27648d_{\mathrm{ff}}=27648, 4040 query heads and 88 key-value heads of dimension dh=128d_{h}=128, and a vocabulary of 152,064152{,}064 tokens. Section 5.6 extends F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} to Qwen3 [Y+25], which normalizes queries and keys per head and, in its mixture-of-experts models, routes each token to a few of many MLPs. F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} has no floating-point step and no data-dependent loop. Every operation below is an exact integer definition. The weights and embeddings are fixed by CWC_{W}, and every other constant (exponents, shifts, biases and the contents of the tables) by the circuit digest hcirch_{\mathrm{circ}} of the statement (Section 7.6).

5.1 Number formats

  • •

    Residual stream. Integers in A=[−223,223)A=[-2^{23},2^{23}) with fh=10f_{h}=10 fractional bits.

  • •

    Matrix-product inputs. A row of activations is quantized to integers in [−127,127][-127,127] with one power-of-two exponent per row, chosen as the least exponent at which the row fits (𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝖺𝗇𝗍𝟪\mathsf{Requant8} below).

  • •

    Weights. Integers in [−127,127][-127,127] with one power-of-two exponent per output column (or per tensor).

  • •

    Scales off the reduction axis. In every product C=A​BC=AB, the scale of AA depends only on the row and the scale of BB only on the column, so the accumulator ∑tam​t​bt​n\sum_{t}a_{mt}b_{tn} is an exact integer and the combined scale is applied once, by a shift, after the sum.

  • •

    Queries, keys and values. Static per-head exponents ehQ,egK,egVe^{Q}_{h},e^{K}_{g},e^{V}_{g} with ehQ+eg⁡(h)K=Eattne^{Q}_{h}+e^{K}_{g(h)}=E_{\mathrm{attn}} for one global constant, so that one exponential table serves every head and layer.

Every exact sum in a linear layer has at most 2152^{15} terms of magnitude at most 1272127^{2}, so |acc|<229|\mathrm{acc}|<2^{29}.

Let aa be a row of integers.

5.6 Qwen3: QK-norm and mixture of experts

We also define F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} for two Qwen3 models [Y+25]. Qwen3-32B is dense: L=64L=64, d=5120d=5120, dff=25600d_{\mathrm{ff}}=25600, 6464 query heads and 88 key-value heads of dimension 128128, and 151,936151{,}936 vocabulary rows. Qwen3-30B-A3B is a mixture of experts: L=48L=48, d=2048d=2048, 3232 query heads and 44 key-value heads, and in every layer 128128 expert MLPs of width de=768d_{e}=768, of which each token uses k=8k=8. Both drop the query, key and value biases (b=0b=0 in 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪𝖲\mathsf{ShiftQ8S}) and add two operations.

QK-norm.

Qwen3 applies RMSNorm with a learned gain to each query and key head before RoPE. Row clamps.

The max⁡(⋅,1)\max(\cdot,1) and min⁡(⋅,24)\min(\cdot,24) above, and Kg​lK_{gl} in the dense gate, define rows whose exponent EhE_{h} is unusually small. Such rows arise for a handful of under-trained tokens at the first position, whose residual has a tiny norm; without the clamps their shifts leave the ranges of the gadgets and F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is undefined on any prompt that starts with them. A clamp changes no row on which the unclamped shift is in range.

5.7 From a checkpoint to F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}

A deterministic program maps a BF16 checkpoint to the integer model. It multiplies the residual basis by a fixed random orthogonal matrix RR (generated from a public seed), as in QuaRot [AMC+24], which spreads activation outliers across channels without changing the floating-point function; fuses each RMSNorm gain and RR into the adjacent weight matrices; and quantizes each weight matrix to 8 bits with per-column power-of-two exponents. It then fixes the static exponents (ehQ,egK,egV,Eattne^{Q}_{h},e^{K}_{g},e^{V}_{g},E_{\mathrm{attn}}, the SiLU input and output units eG,eAe_{G},e_{A}, and the per-layer shift constants) by a two-pass calibration on 1,024 tokens of English technical text (the beginning of a LaTeX document, an early specification of this system), choosing each exponent from the largest magnitude it must represent. For models with QK-norm, one more choice matters. The attention exponent EattnE_{\mathrm{attn}} is set by the head that needs the most range, so in most key-value groups ehQ+egK=Eattne^{Q}_{h}+e^{K}_{g}=E_{\mathrm{attn}} leaves slack: egKe^{K}_{g} may lie anywhere between the least exponent that fits 1.25​max⁡|K|1.25\max|K| and Eattn−maxh⁡ehQE_{\mathrm{attn}}-\max_{h}e^{Q}_{h}, the largest that still lets every query head of the group fit. Giving all of the slack to KK leaves the normalized keys with about 2 of their 8 bits in most Qwen3 layers. The program instead picks, per group, the egKe^{K}_{g} in this range that minimizes the rounding noise of the scores, ∑h∈g(4ehQ​‖Kg‖2+4egK​‖Qh‖2)\sum_{h\in g}\big(4^{e^{Q}_{h}}\|K_{g}\|^{2}+4^{e^{K}_{g}}\|Q_{h}\|^{2}\big) where ehQ=Eattn−egKe^{Q}_{h}=E_{\mathrm{attn}}-e^{K}_{g} and ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|^{2} are mean squares over the calibration text. We call this the Q/K split. This moves only calibration constants: EattnE_{\mathrm{attn}}, the exponential table and every bound of Section 6 stay the same, and so do the proof’s size and cost. We did not apply the split to Qwen2.5, which has no QK-norm; its model gives all of the slack to KK. The first position of a prompt attends only to itself, so its activations depend on the token alone, and some tokens there carry far larger activations than any row of the text. The program therefore runs every vocabulary token at position 0, widens eGe_{G} and eAe_{A} to the largest gate input and SiLU output it sees, lowers the residual’s fractional bits fhf_{h} until every output of the attention and down projections lies in AA, and repeats until nothing changes. Finally it raises the weight exponent of every Wq​k​vW_{qkv} column nn with kmax​(bn)−κnk_{\max}(b_{n})-\kappa_{n} below the largest row exponent EhE_{h} that 𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖲𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖾\mathsf{NormScale} can produce (66 for d=5120d=5120), by the missing amount, and requantizes those columns, so that Kq​sK_{qs} never binds and the shift condition of 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪𝖲\mathsf{ShiftQ8S} holds on every input; it does the same for every gate column (or expert) whose shift could exceed 15. For Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct the sweep changes nothing, and the refit changes 134 of the 458,752 QKV columns, in layers 1 and 2, by one or two bits. For Qwen3-32B the sweep lowers fhf_{h} from 10 to 8 and raises eG,eAe_{G},e_{A} by one, and the refit changes 12,936 of the 1,638,400 gate columns; for Qwen3-30B-A3B the sweep and the refits change nothing.

Where F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is undefined.

Three conditions of the definition are not implied by the formats, and F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is undefined on inputs that violate one: the SiLU input |c|≤214|c|\leq 2^{14} with gate shift kg≤15k_{g}\leq 15; the shifts of the attention output and down projection in [−16,24][-16,24]; and, for a left shift, an output in AA. QK-norm adds one: the unclamped head shift must satisfy κhn+E2≥−31\kappa^{n}_{h}+E_{2}\geq-31, the range of its clamp in the proof (real rows have kn≥4k_{n}\geq 4). A mixture-of-experts layer adds two: the router shift kr≤14k_{r}\leq 14 and the slot alignment ϵ−ϵs≤24\epsilon-\epsilon_{s}\leq 24. The upper bounds on the gate and QK-norm shifts hold on every input by the refits above. An honest prover detects the violation and aborts. The calibration sets the static exponents with margin, and Section 11.9 measures how often an input reaches these limits on real and adversarial text. The program, its seed and its calibration data are published with CWC_{W}, so anyone can recompute CWC_{W} from an open checkpoint. The program uses floating point (32-bit matrix products for the rotation and the weight scales, rounded half to even), so a recomputation on other hardware can differ in rare ties; the integer model it produced, fixed by CWC_{W} and hcirch_{\mathrm{circ}}, is what defines F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}, and quantization is outside F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}. For Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct the program takes under four minutes on one GPU: 17 s to quantize the weights, 13 s to calibrate and refit, and the rest to load the checkpoint and save the result; two runs give bit-identical models.

Lemma 5.1 (Determinism).

For every prompt, seed and policy on which F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is defined, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} has exactly one output, and every intermediate value it defines lies in the range stated for it above.

Proof sketch.

Each operation is a composition of integer additions, products, floor divisions by powers of two, table lookups and clipping, with no choice. The ranges follow from the bounds stated with each operation: 𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝖺𝗇𝗍𝟪\mathsf{Requant8} never clips by its half-open interval, the attention bounds follow from τexp≤210\tau_{\exp}\leq 2^{10} and the block size, and 𝖲𝖺𝗍𝖠𝖽𝖽\mathsf{SatAdd} clips the residual into AA. Section A.6 lists the bounds. ∎

6 A wrap-free constraint system

Each operation of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is proved by a gadget: committed witness columns, polynomial constraints that must vanish row by row, and lookups into a fixed table. The design rule is that every constraint, read as an identity over ℤ\mathbb{Z} on values that satisfy the gadget’s lookups, has both sides below pp in absolute value, and below 230.92^{30.9} except where a bias enters (𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪𝖲\mathsf{ShiftQ8S}). The identity then holds in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} exactly when it holds in ℤ\mathbb{Z} (Lemma 6.1).

6.1 The tagged table

All static lookups go into one table 𝒯\mathcal{T} of 2262^{26} rows and seven columns (tag,v0,…,v5)(\mathrm{tag},v_{0},\ldots,v_{5}), compressed as tag+β1​v0+β2​v1+⋯\mathrm{tag}+\beta_{1}v_{0}+\beta_{2}v_{1}+\cdots. Table 1 lists its tags. A range check u∈[0,2k)u\in[0,2^{k}) is the single lookup (k,u)(k,u), so every bound costs one lookup whatever its width, and the shift-dependent bounds of the rounding gadgets come from one row per shift value. The rows of 𝒯\mathcal{T} are distinct tuples, as Lemma 3.2 requires: within a tag every row has a different key (the value, shift or table input), and the tag separates rows of different tags, so for instance the range rows (k,v)(k,v) for different kk and the same vv are different tuples.

6.2 Rounding gadgets

𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽\mathsf{ShiftRound}.

Inputs: an accumulator acc\mathrm{acc} with |acc|+230+223<p|\mathrm{acc}|+2^{30}+2^{23}<p (in our models |acc|<229|\mathrm{acc}|<2^{29}, and 229.62^{29.6} in a mixture-of-experts down projection) and a per-row shift kk. 6.3 Selected indices and gathers

A gadget that selects one element of a row, such as the minimality witness of 𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝖺𝗇𝗍𝟪\mathsf{Requant8}, commits the index as Boolean bits b1,…,bℓb_{1},\ldots,b_{\ell} with bk​(1−bk)=0b_{k}(1-b_{k})=0 and reads the selected value as the virtual aj∗=∑ieq⁡(b,i)​aia_{j^{\ast}}=\sum_{i}\mathrm{eq}(b,i)\,a_{i}. The Boolean constraints are necessary. For b∉{0,1}ℓb\notin\{0,1\}^{\ell}, the sum is the row’s multilinear extension at bb, which a prover can steer to any value by solving for bb.

The attention row maximum uses a gather instead. Per query row mm and head, the prover commits a key index jm∗j^{\ast}_{m} and the gathered key row Kmg=K^jm∗,⋅K^{g}_{m}=\hat{K}_{j^{\ast}_{m},\cdot}, and per key position jj the number μj\mu_{j} of (row, head) pairs that select it. The gather is a dynamic lookup set with its own tag:

∑m,c1Z−(tag+β1​jm∗+β2​c+β3​Km​cg)=∑j,cμjZ−(tag+β1​j+β2​c+β3​K^j​c).\sum_{m,c}\frac{1}{Z-(\mathrm{tag}+\beta_{1}j^{\ast}_{m}+\beta_{2}c+\beta_{3}K^{g}_{mc})}\;=\;\sum_{j,c}\frac{\mu_{j}}{Z-(\mathrm{tag}+\beta_{1}j+\beta_{2}c+\beta_{3}\hat{K}_{jc})}.

Two range lookups place jm∗j^{\ast}_{m} between the first position of mm’s sequence and mm. The maximum is then Mm=∑cQ^m​c​Km​cgM_{m}=\sum_{c}\hat{Q}_{mc}K^{g}_{mc}, proved by a product sumcheck, and the softmax lookup below forces Mm≥accm​jM_{m}\geq\mathrm{acc}_{mj} for every valid jj. Hence MmM_{m} is the maximum (Lemma A.1). The gather adds dh+2d_{h}+2 committed elements per (row, head) and dhd_{h} per key, in place of the ℓ\ell index bits and an eq\mathrm{eq}-weighted sum over a whole row of scores.

6.4 Attention

The causal score matrix of a head is split into 128×128128\times 128 tiles, and only the tiles on or below the diagonal are kept (Figure 1): 12​(S/128)​(S/128+1)\frac{1}{2}(S/128)(S/128+1) tiles per sequence and head. The probabilities PP are committed per tile. The scores acc\mathrm{acc} are virtual, and so are the block partials N(b)N^{(b)} and the denominators DD.

  1. 1.

    Softmax lookups. For every entry of every kept tile, (𝖤𝖷𝖯,xm​j,Pm​j)∈𝒯(\mathsf{EXP},x_{mj},P_{mj})\in\mathcal{T}, with xm​j=Mm−accm​jx_{mj}=M_{m}-\mathrm{acc}_{mj} on off-diagonal tiles and xm​j=νm​j​(Mm−accm​j)+(1−νm​j)​xminx_{mj}=\nu_{mj}(M_{m}-\mathrm{acc}_{mj})+(1-\nu_{mj})x_{\min} on diagonal tiles, where ν\nu is the public causal mask of a tile and τexp​(xmin)=0\tau_{\exp}(x_{\min})=0. The table’s domain x<223x<2^{23} enforces Mm≥accm​jM_{m}\geq\mathrm{acc}_{mj}, and masked entries read exactly 00. These lookups and nothing else form the tile domain (Section 7.2), with 2142^{14} entries per block and one block per tile.

  2. 2.

    Scores. The domain ends in claims on acc\mathrm{acc} at points inside the tiles. They are reduced to claims on Q^\hat{Q} and K^\hat{K} by one product sumcheck per key-value group over (query row, channel), with the tile structure entering through public weights.

    NN and DD. The rounding of the block partials, Nm​c=∑b𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽⁡(Nm​c(b),km)N_{mc}=\sum_{b}\mathsf{ShiftRound}(N^{(b)}_{mc},k_{m}), yields a claim on the virtual N(b)N^{(b)}, and the normalization of DD yields a claim on DD. Both are proved by one batched sumcheck over the keys jj:

    γ1​∑jP~​(rm,j)​eq​(rb,b⁡(j))​V~​(j,rc)+γ2​∑jP~​(rm′,j)=γ1​N~(⋅)​(rm,rb,rc)+γ2​D~​(rm′).\textstyle\gamma_{1}\sum_{j}\widetilde{P}(r_{m},j)\,\mathrm{eq}\big(r_{b},b(j)\big)\,\widetilde{V}(j,r_{c})+\gamma_{2}\sum_{j}\widetilde{P}(r^{\prime}_{m},j)\;=\;\gamma_{1}\widetilde{N}^{(\cdot)}(r_{m},r_{b},r_{c})+\gamma_{2}\widetilde{D}(r^{\prime}_{m}).

    Since blocks are aligned to 2122^{12} keys, b⁡(j)b(j) is the high bits of jj, and eq⁡(rb,b⁡(j))\mathrm{eq}(r_{b},b(j)) is a public table.

Dm=2Em​δm+ρmD_{m}=2^{E_{m}}\delta_{m}+\rho_{m} by the signed normalization gadget, with Em∈[−5,14]E_{m}\in[-5,14] by two range lookups; km=max⁡(7,Em)k_{m}=\max(7,E_{m}) by a flag fm=[Em≥7]f_{m}=[E_{m}\geq 7], fixed by (4,fm​(Em−7)+(1−fm)​(6−Em))∈𝒯(4,f_{m}(E_{m}-7)+(1-f_{m})(6-E_{m}))\in\mathcal{T}; (22,(1−fm)​Dm)∈𝒯(22,(1-f_{m})D_{m})\in\mathcal{T}, which plays the role of 𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖲𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖾\mathsf{NormScale}’s input bound: every left shift has Dm<222D_{m}<2^{22}, so 2Em−​Dm<227<p2^{E_{m}^{-}}D_{m}<2^{27}<p at every SS, and an honest Dm<222D_{m}<2^{22} is exactly the case Em<7E_{m}<7; (𝖱𝖤𝖢𝖨𝖯,δm−215,recipm)∈𝒯(\mathsf{RECIP},\delta_{m}-2^{15},\mathrm{recip}_{m})\in\mathcal{T}; and o=𝖬𝗎𝗅𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽⁡(N,recip,25+Em−km+sh)o=\mathsf{MulRound}(N,\mathrm{recip},25+E_{m}-k_{m}+s_{h}).

A linear layer with weight WW and input qq reduces a claim acc~​(ro,rm)=v\widetilde{\mathrm{acc}}(r_{o},r_{m})=v by the product sumcheck ∑tq~​(t,rm)​W~​(ro,t)=v\sum_{t}\widetilde{q}(t,r_{m})\,\widetilde{W}(r_{o},t)=v. Weights are committed in blocks of 210×2102^{10}\times 2^{10}; at the end the prover sends the value of every weight block at the final point, and the verifier checks their combination against the sumcheck’s final claim. 6.6 Qwen3: QK-norm, router and experts

QK-norm.

A query or key head row is dh=128d_{h}=128 consecutive columns of the QKV accumulator, inside one column block. Each expert product is a gathered sumcheck. 6.7 Determinism and no wrap

Lemma 6.1 (No wrap).

Every constraint of this section, read as a polynomial identity over ℤ\mathbb{Z} in variables that satisfy the gadget’s lookups, has absolute value below pp: below 230.92^{30.9} for every gadget (Table 18) except 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪𝖲\mathsf{ShiftQ8S}, whose bound depends on the bias through kmaxk_{\max}. Hence the identity holds in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} if and only if it holds in ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Lemma 6.2 (Determinism).

Fix the public inputs and committed weights of a valid model: weights in [−127,127][-127,127] and embedding rows in AA. For inputs in range, every gadget has exactly one assignment of its output columns that satisfies its constraints, and it equals the definition of Section 5. Consequently, a full assignment that satisfies all constraints, lookups and gathers is the execution of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}.

Section A.6 gives the bounds and the proofs. Both lemmas are statements about the constraint system alone; Section 8 combines them with the soundness of the protocol.

Remark 6.3 (Left shifts).

Without the 𝖲𝖱𝖠\mathsf{SRA} bound, cc would be the unique element of AA congruent to 2−k​acc2^{-k}\mathrm{acc}, which equals the left shift of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} whenever the latter lies in AA. On inputs where 2−k​acc∉A2^{-k}\mathrm{acc}\notin A, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is undefined and an honest prover aborts, yet the two 𝖲𝖱\mathsf{SR} lookups could accept such a residue. A cheating prover could exploit this: during development, before the bound was added, a randomized search over accumulators constructed such residues. The bound closes the gap, and a regression test (Section 11.10) checks that the forged rows are rejected. The regime k=0k=0 is safe even without it, since |acc−c|<229.6+223<p|\mathrm{acc}-c|<2^{29.6}+2^{23}<p. For Qwen2.5-32B, the static parts of the shifts are at least 88 for the attention output, 1414 for the down projection and 11 for the logits, so a negative shift needs a row exponent above these constants.

7 The protocol

7.1 Overview

The prover makes two passes over the model (Figure 2). The commit pass runs F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} forward, one layer at a time. For each layer it builds the witness from the layer’s input, commits it, and counts the table multiplicities of its lookups. It keeps only the residual stream between layers, in host memory. After the last layer it commits the output gadgets and the multiplicity columns, and the transcript then yields the lookup challenges (Z,β)(Z,\beta). The prove pass visits the model backward, from the sampling constraints to the embedding. Each layer’s witness is recomputed from its stored input. The layer’s sumchecks consume the claims that later layers made on its output and produce claims on its input, on its weights and on its own committed tensors. A final phase opens every committed tensor at the points the claims name.

The protocol has three building blocks: domains (Section 7.2), which prove constraints and lookups on a set of columns; the LogUp table side with chunked multiplicities (Section 7.3); and a multilinear commitment for all committed tensors (Section 7.5). Product sumchecks and the attention reductions of Section 6 connect them.

7.2 Domains

A domain has KK blocks of 2n2^{n} rows and a set of columns. A column is full (one value per row and block), a row column (constant along its low cc variables), or a column column (depending only on the low cc variables, possibly shared by all blocks). Each column has a role: committed (its claims go to the commitment), virtual (its claims go to the protocol that defines it, such as a product sumcheck), or public (the verifier evaluates it, in closed form where possible). A domain carries constraints C1,…,CsC_{1},\ldots,C_{s}, polynomials in the columns, and lookups ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\ldots,L, each with a numerator NℓN_{\ell} (default 11) and a tuple (tℓ,vℓ,0,…)(t_{\ell},v_{\ell,0},\ldots) of polynomials in the columns, whose compressed denominator is

Qℓ​(x)=Z−(tℓ​(x)+∑iβi+1​vℓ,i​(x)).Q_{\ell}(x)=Z-\Big(t_{\ell}(x)+\sum_{i}\beta_{i+1}v_{\ell,i}(x)\Big).

The domain asserts that every CkC_{k} vanishes on every row and that the root fractions (Pℓ,Qℓ)(P_{\ell},Q_{\ell}) it sends equal ∑xNℓ​(x)/Qℓ​(x)\sum_{x}N_{\ell}(x)/Q_{\ell}(x).

For each lookup, the fraction tree pairs rows along the top in-block variable xn−1x_{n-1}. With y∈{0,1}n−1y\in\{0,1\}^{n-1} and Nh​(y)=N​(y,h)N^{h}(y)=N(y,h), the layer just above the leaves is

pℓ​(y)=Nℓ0​(y)​Qℓ1​(y)+Nℓ1​(y)​Qℓ0​(y),qℓ​(y)=Qℓ0​(y)​Qℓ1​(y).p_{\ell}(y)=N^{0}_{\ell}(y)Q^{1}_{\ell}(y)+N^{1}_{\ell}(y)Q^{0}_{\ell}(y),\qquad q_{\ell}(y)=Q^{0}_{\ell}(y)\,Q^{1}_{\ell}(y).

The domain protocol (for K=1K=1; blocks add one phase of block variables) is:

  1. 1.

    The prover sends the root fractions. Batched GKR over all LL trees reduces them, layer by layer, to claims pℓ​(r)=πℓp_{\ell}(r)=\pi_{\ell} and qℓ​(r)=κℓq_{\ell}(r)=\kappa_{\ell} at one random point r∈𝔽p4n−1r\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}^{n-1}.

  2. 2.

    The verifier draws a1,…,aL,λ,γ1,…,γs,η∈𝔽p4a_{1},\ldots,a_{L},\lambda,\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{s},\eta\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}. One sumcheck over y∈{0,1}n−1y\in\{0,1\}^{n-1} proves

    ∑yeq⁡(r,y)​[∑ℓaℓ​(pℓ​(y)+λ​qℓ​(y))+∑kγk​(Ck0​(y)+η​Ck1​(y))]=∑ℓaℓ​(πℓ+λ​κℓ),\sum_{y}\mathrm{eq}(r,y)\Big[\sum_{\ell}a_{\ell}\big(p_{\ell}(y)+\lambda\,q_{\ell}(y)\big)+\sum_{k}\gamma_{k}\big(C^{0}_{k}(y)+\eta\,C^{1}_{k}(y)\big)\Big]=\sum_{\ell}a_{\ell}(\pi_{\ell}+\lambda\kappa_{\ell}), (1)

    where pℓp_{\ell}, qℓq_{\ell} and CkhC^{h}_{k} are expanded as polynomials in the half-columns fjh​(y)=fj​(y,h)f^{h}_{j}(y)=f_{j}(y,h).

  3. 3.

    The sumcheck ends at a point ρ\rho; the prover sends fj0​(ρ)f^{0}_{j}(\rho) and fj1​(ρ)f^{1}_{j}(\rho) for every column, and the verifier evaluates the bracket of (1) on them.

  4. 4.

    The verifier draws tt, and each column receives the claim f~j​(ρ,t)=(1−t)​fj0​(ρ)+t​fj1​(ρ)\widetilde{f}_{j}(\rho,t)=(1-t)f^{0}_{j}(\rho)+tf^{1}_{j}(\rho), routed according to its role.

Lemma 7.1 (Domain).

Suppose the columns are fixed before rr is drawn, and that some constraint is nonzero on some row or some root fraction differs from the fraction sum of its leaves. Then, except with probability at most ϵGKR+(n+1)/|𝔽p4|+ϵsc+1/|𝔽p4|\epsilon_{\mathrm{GKR}}+(n+1)/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|+\epsilon_{\mathrm{sc}}+1/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|, the verifier rejects or one of the column claims of step 4 is false. Here ϵGKR\epsilon_{\mathrm{GKR}} is the error of the GKR layers and ϵsc≤(n−1)​(d+1)/|𝔽p4|\epsilon_{\mathrm{sc}}\leq(n-1)(d+1)/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}| that of the final sumcheck, whose bracket has degree dd.

The proof is in Section A.3. Merging the GKR leaf layer into the zerocheck saves one sumcheck per domain and lets the leaf expressions be arbitrary polynomials in the columns: a remainder such as acc+2k−1−2k​c\mathrm{acc}+2^{k-1}-2^{k}c never needs its own column. The cost is a higher degree: a constraint of degree 3 and a lookup tuple of degree 2 give a bracket of degree up to 6 in the half-columns. Our largest domains have degree 8 to 10.

Domains with the same number of variables are proved together as blocks of one domain where possible. For attention, each kept tile is a block of 2142^{14} rows, and the block index is bound after the in-block variables, so that every column ends in a single claim at a point (in-tile point, tile point).

7.3 Chunked LogUp and the table side

Every static lookup (a lookup into 𝒯\mathcal{T}) is assigned, in commit order, to a chunk of at most 2302^{30} lookups; a domain’s lookups are never split across chunks. Chunk ii has its own multiplicity column mi∈[0,230)226m_{i}\in[0,2^{30})^{2^{26}}, committed with the trace. The prover sends the assignment before ZZ is drawn. At the end of the prove pass the verifier sums the root fractions of the lookups of chunk ii into SiS_{i}, draws γ1,γ2,…\gamma_{1},\gamma_{2},\ldots, and one GKR over the table proves

∑v∈𝒯∑iγi​mi​(v)Z−𝒯⁡(v)=∑iγi​Si,\sum_{v\in\mathcal{T}}\frac{\sum_{i}\gamma_{i}\,m_{i}(v)}{Z-\mathcal{T}(v)}\;=\;\sum_{i}\gamma_{i}S_{i},

ending in claims on every mim_{i} and on the seven table columns at one point.

Lemma 7.2 (Chunks).

Suppose every root fraction equals the fraction sum of its lookups, and some static lookup is outside 𝒯\mathcal{T}. Then, except with probability at most ϵLU+1/|𝔽p4|+ϵGKR\epsilon_{\mathrm{LU}}+1/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|+\epsilon_{\mathrm{GKR}}, the verifier rejects or one of the claims on the multiplicity or table columns is false. Here ϵLU\epsilon_{\mathrm{LU}} bounds the probability that the fraction identity of one chunk holds at a random (Z,β)(Z,\beta) although its multisets differ (Lemma 8.1).

The proof is in Section A.4. The chunk bound is a soundness condition: a proof of a 16,384-token sequence through Qwen2.5-32B makes about 7×10117\times 10^{11} lookups, more than 300​p300p, so a single multiplicity column would allow pp copies of an out-of-table value to cancel. The table side costs one GKR over 2262^{26} leaves for all chunks together, and one committed column per chunk.

Gathers and other dynamic lookups form separate sets, identified by their tags, whose fraction sums over all domains must be zero. Their counts are below pp by construction (a gather of dhd_{h} values for every (row, head) pair of one key-value group).

7.4 Work units and the routing of claims

The committed tensors of a layer are grouped into units, each owned by the step of the protocol that consumes it first in forward order: 𝗂𝗇\mathsf{in} (normalization and quantization of the residual, Q,K,VQ,K,V, RoPE), 𝖺𝗍𝗍.g\mathsf{att}.g for each key-value group gg (the probabilities PP, gathered keys, rounded block partials), 𝖺𝗈\mathsf{ao} (softmax normalization, 𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝖺𝗇𝗍𝟪\mathsf{Requant8} of the attention output, output projection, residual), 𝗆𝗂\mathsf{mi} (normalization before the MLP), 𝗆𝗅𝗉.s\mathsf{mlp}.s for slices ss of the MLP width, and 𝗆𝗈\mathsf{mo} (down projection, residual). Weights form one unit per layer, plus units for the embedding and the output head. Two fixed units hold public data that every proof for a model and shape reuses: the lookup table 𝒯\mathcal{T} and the RoPE tables.

A claim is a point and a value per block of a tensor, or a point with weights over the blocks and one value. Claims accumulate on their tensor until every protocol step that reads the unit has run; then the unit is opened (Section 7.5). The prove pass visits steps in reverse forward order, so a unit’s last claim arrives in the step that owns it.

7.5 The commitment

All committed tensors, across all units, are committed with one multilinear polynomial commitment scheme and opened by one evaluation proof at the end.

Columns and packing.

A tensor of KK blocks of 2c02^{c_{0}} values is packed into columns of 2c2^{c} values, c∈[5,23]c\in[5,23]. The packer picks the largest cc whose zero padding stays below 10%10\% of the tensor or below 2202^{20} elements (15%15\% for weights). Columns of length 2c2^{c} form the class cc of their unit. Every query of the evaluation proof opens every column, so the number of columns, more than the number of committed elements, sets the proof size and the verifier’s hashing. Wide columns are therefore preferred even at some cost in padding.

Encoding and leaves.

Each column of class cc is encoded in RS⁡[c+1]\mathrm{RS}[c+1] (rate 1/21/2, codewords of at most 2242^{24} symbols). A leaf of class cc holds four consecutive codeword positions of every column of the class, and is hashed with BLAKE3 in chunks of 6464 columns whose digests are chained. A query thus opens all columns at four positions, which also covers the first two folds.

Mixed-height Merkle trees.

The units of one layer form a set, committed one after another with leaf digests chained across units. A set’s classes share one tree, built over the leaves of its largest class cmc_{m} (Figure 3). The leaf digest of a smaller class cc enters at the level that has 2c−12^{c-1} nodes: a node there is 𝖧(𝖧(ℓ∥r)∥leafc)\mathsf{H}(\mathsf{H}(\ell\|r)\,\|\,\mathrm{leaf}_{c}). A query position qq at the largest class corresponds to position q≫(cm−c)q\gg(c_{m}-c) at class cc, so one path serves every class of the set. Classes with fewer than 272^{7} leaves lie entirely inside the cap and keep separate trees. Each tree sends its cap of 272^{7} nodes.

Opening a unit.

When a unit’s claims are complete, the prover reduces them, per class, to a single point: one sumcheck in 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} proves ∑x∑ieq⁡(zi,x)​gi​(x)\sum_{x}\sum_{i}\mathrm{eq}(z_{i},x)\,g_{i}(x) equal to the combined claim, where claim ii has point ziz_{i} and gig_{i} is a random combination of the columns it touches. At the final point ρ\rho, the prover sends f~k​(ρ)\widetilde{f}_{k}(\rho) for every column of the class, the verifier checks the reduction, draws αk′∈𝔽p8\alpha^{\prime}_{k}\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}, and records the claim y=g~​(ρ)y=\widetilde{g}(\rho) for g=∑kαk′​fkg=\sum_{k}\alpha^{\prime}_{k}f_{k}.

Batching claims at different points.

Let NVN_{V} be the largest class plus one, and x[c]x_{[c]} the top cc coordinates of x∈{0,1}NVx\in\{0,1\}^{N_{V}}. Given claims (ρt,yt)(\rho_{t},y_{t}) on combined columns gtg_{t} of classes ctc_{t}, the verifier draws λt∈𝔽p8\lambda_{t}\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}, and a sumcheck over NVN_{V} variables proves

∑x∈{0,1}NV∑tλt​eq​(ρt,x[ct])​g~t​(x[ct])=∑t2NV−ct​λt​yt.\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^{N_{V}}}\sum_{t}\lambda_{t}\,\mathrm{eq}(\rho_{t},x_{[c_{t}]})\,\widetilde{g}_{t}(x_{[c_{t}]})=\sum_{t}2^{N_{V}-c_{t}}\lambda_{t}\,y_{t}. (2)

It ends at a point rr with the claim ∑cHc​(r[c])=V\sum_{c}H_{c}(r_{[c]})=V, where Hc=∑t∈class ​cλt​eq​(ρt,r[c])​gtH_{c}=\sum_{t\in\text{class }c}\lambda_{t}\mathrm{eq}(\rho_{t},r_{[c]})\,g_{t} is a fixed linear combination of the committed columns of class cc. The prover runs its first 12 rounds on the vectors gt​(⋅,ρt,hi)g_{t}(\cdot,\rho_{t,\mathrm{hi}}) of at most 2122^{12} entries, kept from the unit openings; the remaining rounds need gt​(rlo,⋅)g_{t}(r_{\mathrm{lo}},\cdot), and forming HcH_{c} needs every gtg_{t} in full.

Per-layer reduction.

Applied once to all units of the proof, (2) would need every gtg_{t} at the end of the proof, when the witness is no longer resident, and the prover would have to rebuild every layer’s witness twice more. Instead, the units of one layer (its groups and its weights) form a segment. When the segment’s last unit has been opened, at the end of the layer’s prove pass, the prover still holds every gtg_{t} of the layer, and runs (2) over the segment’s units alone. This is a sumcheck over 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}, like every instance of (2); it is a different step from the point reduction of a unit opening above, which runs over 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} and precedes the draw of the αk′∈𝔽p8\alpha^{\prime}_{k}\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}. It sends ys,c=Hc(s)​(r[c](s))y_{s,c}=H^{(s)}_{c}(r^{(s)}_{[c]}) for each class, and the verifier checks ∑cys,c=Vs\sum_{c}y_{s,c}=V_{s}. The prover keeps Hc(s)H^{(s)}_{c}, one vector per class instead of one per unit, in pinned host memory.

The global evaluation proof.

After the prove pass, (2) runs once more over the units outside segments (the output gadgets, the embedding and output head, the fixed units and the multiplicity columns) and one pseudo-unit per (segment, class), with claim (r[c](s),ys,c)(r^{(s)}_{[c]},y_{s,c}) on Hc(s)H^{(s)}_{c}. The prover reads the pseudo-units’ vectors back from host memory, so no layer’s witness is rebuilt for this step. The result is again a claim ∑cHc​(r[c])=V\sum_{c}H_{c}(r_{[c]})=V with HcH_{c} a fixed linear combination of committed columns: the coefficient of a column of a segment unit tt is the product of the two levels’ factors λ′​eq​(r[c](s),r[c])⋅λt​eq​(ρt,r[c](s))⋅αt,k′\lambda^{\prime}\mathrm{eq}(r^{(s)}_{[c]},r_{[c]})\cdot\lambda_{t}\mathrm{eq}(\rho_{t},r^{(s)}_{[c]})\cdot\alpha^{\prime}_{t,k}. BaseFold proves this claim by folding a single codeword, to which class cc’s combined codeword is added at level NV−cN_{V}-c, as in batched FRI for mixed degrees. The level at which each class enters, like the class sizes themselves, is computed by the verifier from the shape in the statement (and so bound by hcirch_{\mathrm{circ}}); the prover cannot choose it. A fold oracle is committed at every second level, and the last message of 252^{5} symbols is sent in the clear. After a 30-bit proof of work, 153153 query positions are drawn; class cc opens the leaf at q≫(NV−c)q\gg(N_{V}-c), and the oracle at level LL opens the leaf at q≫Lq\gg L. Lemma 8.3 states the soundness of this construction.

Weights and fixed units.

CWC_{W} is a SHA-256 hash of the caps of the weight units. Weights are committed once per model and shape; each proof reopens them as part of the global evaluation proof, so a proof pays for reducing and opening the weights while their encoding is reused. The fixed units are checked the same way against digests computed once per model and shape. The verifier therefore never evaluates the 2262^{26}-row table or the RoPE tables itself. It receives their evaluations as claims that the commitment opens.

7.6 Transcript and statement

The transcript starts by absorbing the statement: a protocol tag, the policy, CWC_{W}, a digest hcirch_{\mathrm{circ}} of the circuit description (model configuration, shapes, and every constant of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} outside CWC_{W}: the exponents, shifts and biases of every layer and the contents of τexp\tau_{\exp}, τSiLU\tau_{\mathrm{SiLU}}, the RoPE tables and τexp,θ\tau_{\exp,\theta}), 𝖲𝖧𝖠𝟤𝟧𝟨⁡(x)\mathsf{SHA256}(x), 𝖲𝖧𝖠𝟤𝟧𝟨⁡(y)\mathsf{SHA256}(y), ncn_{c}, the length SS, and a 256-bit salt chosen by the prover and given to the verifier. The salt has no role in soundness, which holds for every salt under the bound on random-oracle queries; it is reserved for a hiding mode, in which it makes the transcript of a repeated statement unpredictable, and our proofs set it to zero. Challenges are drawn in this order, each after everything it tests has been absorbed:

  1. 1.

    caps of every unit, the chunk assignment and the multiplicity caps; an 11-bit proof-of-work nonce;

  2. 2.

    ZZ and the tuple coefficients β=(β1,…,β8)\beta=(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{8});

  3. 3.

    per domain and sumcheck: GKR and sumcheck round challenges after each round message, and the batching coefficients of Section 7.2;

  4. 4.

    per unit opening: point-reduction coefficients in 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} and column coefficients α′\alpha^{\prime} in 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}};

  5. 5.

    λt\lambda_{t}, the global sumcheck and fold challenges in 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}, a 30-bit proof-of-work nonce, and the query positions.

The final query openings (leaf values and Merkle paths) are appended to the proof without being absorbed, since no challenge is drawn after them. A challenge coordinate is sampled by rejection: 31-bit words of the hash output are drawn until one is below pp, so the number of compressions per challenge depends on the data. The host verifier, the host prover and the warp-level device transcript run the same rejection loop on the same bytes, so they draw identical challenges; the tests check that the host and device transcripts produce byte-identical proofs.

7.7 The verifier

The verifier recomputes the seed and the sampling values utu_{t}, checks that every token lies in the vocabulary, checks the policy, the stopping rule on yy and that the generated tokens are the fed-back ones, and replays the transcript. The cheap checks come first: the statement and policy checks before the transcript starts, and the caps of the weight and fixed units against CWC_{W} and the fixed digests before any sumcheck, so a proof for other weights or tables fails before any expensive work. It checks every sumcheck and GKR round, the per-chunk and per-set fraction sums, the claims on public columns (index columns, causal masks, one-hot and prefix indicators of the targets, all in closed form with O⁡(log)O(\log) work), the caps of the weight and fixed units against CWC_{W} and the fixed digests, the unit openings, the global sumcheck, the folds, both proof-of-work nonces, and every query. Some model constants (biases, per-layer shift constants, the bounds Kq​sK_{qs} and Kg​mK_{gm}) enter claims that the verifier evaluates directly, since opening them would add columns to every query; hcirch_{\mathrm{circ}} binds them to the statement. The proof is a sequence of byte strings and arrays of field elements in a plain length-prefixed format; the verifier checks every length, shape and Merkle path depth against the values the protocol determines, and every element against pp, before using it.

8 Security

We analyze the interactive oracle proof underlying Sable and obtain the non-interactive argument by the Fiat–Shamir transform. The transcript hash (BLAKE3’s compression function in sequential mode, Section 3.5) is modeled as a random oracle, and BLAKE3 is assumed collision resistant for the Merkle trees, as in deployed hash-based arguments.

8.1 Tuple compression

Lemma 8.1 (Tuple compression).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a multiset of tuples in 𝔽pk+1\mathbb{F}_{p}^{k+1} with |𝒜|<p|\mathcal{A}|<p, let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a set of tuples, and let m:𝒯→𝔽p4m:\mathcal{T}\to\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} be arbitrary. Let DD be the number of distinct tuples in 𝒜∪𝒯\mathcal{A}\cup\mathcal{T}, and for a tuple uu write ϕu​(Z,β)=Z−(u0+β​u1+⋯+βk​uk)\phi_{u}(Z,\beta)=Z-(u_{0}+\beta u_{1}+\cdots+\beta^{k}u_{k}). If some tuple of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is not in 𝒯\mathcal{T}, then for uniform (Z,β)∈𝔽p42(Z,\beta)\in\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}^{2},

Pr[∑u∈𝒜1ϕu​(Z,β)=∑v∈𝒯m⁡(v)ϕv​(Z,β) and all denominators are nonzero]≤k⁡(D−1)|𝔽p4|,\Pr\Big[\sum_{u\in\mathcal{A}}\frac{1}{\phi_{u}(Z,\beta)}=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{T}}\frac{m(v)}{\phi_{v}(Z,\beta)}\text{ and all denominators are nonzero}\Big]\leq\frac{k(D-1)}{|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|},

and some denominator vanishes with probability at most k​D/|𝔽p4|kD/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|. With independent coefficients β1,…,βk\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{k} in place of the powers of β\beta, the bounds become (D−1)/|𝔽p4|(D-1)/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}| and D/|𝔽p4|D/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|.

The proof (Section A.2) treats the identity in the bivariate rational function field 𝔽p4​(Z,β)\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}(Z,\beta), where the ϕu\phi_{u} for distinct tuples are distinct irreducible polynomials, and applies the Schwartz–Zippel lemma to the cleared identity of total degree at most k​DkD. A chunk has D≤230+226D\leq 2^{30}+2^{26} distinct tuples, and our tuples have arity up to 77 (k=6k=6). With powers of one challenge, the lemma would give ϵLU≤2⋅6⋅(230+226)/|𝔽p4|≈2−90.3\epsilon_{\mathrm{LU}}\leq 2\cdot 6\cdot(2^{30}+2^{26})/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|\approx 2^{-90.3}. Sable draws one challenge per coordinate (β1,…,β8\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{8}), so ϵLU≤2​(230+226)/|𝔽p4|≈2−92.9\epsilon_{\mathrm{LU}}\leq 2(2^{30}+2^{26})/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}|\approx 2^{-92.9}, at no measurable cost: the coefficients are a handful of extension elements per proof. The 11-bit proof of work before (Z,β)(Z,\beta) multiplies the cost of each attempt by 2112^{11}, which gives 2−103.92^{-103.9} in the convention of Table 2.

8.2 The commitment

Lemma 8.2 (Mixed-height trees).

For a mixed-height tree, an algorithm that outputs two valid openings of the same query position of the same class to different leaf contents, under the same cap, yields a BLAKE3 collision.

Proof.

Both openings recompute the path from the leaf digest to the cap, injecting the digests of the other classes at their fixed levels. The cap node is the same, so walking down from it, the first level at which the two computations differ yields two different inputs with the same BLAKE3 output. The level at which each class enters is a function of the class sizes alone, so both computations inject at the same levels. If the leaf contents differ, then the chained leaf digests differ or collide, so a difference exists at some level. ∎

Lemma 8.3 (Evaluation proof).

Assume the trees are binding. If some recorded claim (ρt,yt)(\rho_{t},y_{t}) is false for every codeword close to the committed oracles, then the verifier of the global evaluation proof accepts with probability at most ϵprox+(ρ+η)q⋅2−30+ϵsc,8\epsilon_{\mathrm{prox}}+(\sqrt{\rho}+\eta)^{q}\cdot 2^{-30}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{sc},8}, with ρ=1/2\rho=1/2, q=153q=153 queries and a 30-bit proof of work, where ϵprox\epsilon_{\mathrm{prox}} is the correlated-agreement error for affine spaces in the Johnson regime [BSCI+20, Thm. 1.6] over 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}} for codewords of at most 2242^{24} symbols and ϵsc,8\epsilon_{\mathrm{sc},8} the error of the sumchecks over 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}.

Which theorem this uses.

The original analysis of BaseFold [ZCF24] is in the unique-decoding regime. The list-decoding regime, which our 153 queries need, is analyzed for BaseFold over Reed–Solomon codes by Haböck [Hab24], through a correlated-agreement theorem for linear subcodes of Reed–Solomon codes that generalizes the one of BCIKS. Our evaluation proof differs from the protocol analyzed there in three ways, and the argument below rests on the following conditions.

  1. 1.

    Mixed lengths. The combined codeword of class cc enters the folding at level NV−cN_{V}-c with fresh coefficients α′\alpha^{\prime} (and λ\lambda) in 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}, drawn after the class’s columns are committed, as in batched FRI for mixed degrees. At such a level the word that is folded next is an affine combination, with independent uniform coefficients, of the folded word and the new class’s columns, all of the same length, so the affine-space correlated-agreement bound applies to that level’s words. At most 1919 classes enter (252^{5} to 2232^{23}), so a union bound over the entry levels costs at most log2⁡19<4.3\log_{2}19<4.3 bits of the proximity term.

  2. 2.

    Two folds per oracle. A fold oracle is committed at every second level, so the queries check a fold of four symbols by two challenges. We treat it as two consecutive binary folds, each by a uniform challenge drawn after the word it folds is fixed; the intermediate word is not committed but is a fixed function of committed oracles, and the query check verifies the composition. Each binary fold is a line through two words, to which the line version of correlated agreement applies.

  3. 3.

    Batching with the sumcheck. The folding challenges are the challenges of the evaluation sumcheck over 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}, as in BaseFold, so the sumcheck terms (ϵsc,8\epsilon_{\mathrm{sc},8}) and the proximity terms are separate rows of Table 2.

We are not aware of a published theorem that covers exactly this combination of the list-decoding regime, mixed-length batching at later levels and two folds per oracle. The argument below composes the BCIKS correlated-agreement theorems round by round, as analyses of batched FRI do, and it is the one step of our soundness analysis that is not a direct application of a stated theorem. The proximity term has a wide margin (163.6163.6 bits against the 103.4103.4 bits of the query term), so the conclusion is not sensitive to the union bounds above. The per-layer reductions of Section 7.5 insert one more sumcheck of degree 2 over 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}} between a unit’s claims and the global evaluation proof: a false claim (ρt,yt)(\rho_{t},y_{t}) of a segment unit makes the segment’s batched claim false except with probability 1/|𝔽p8|1/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}| over the λt\lambda_{t}, and the sumcheck then ends in a false value ys,cy_{s,c} for some class except with probability 2​NV/|𝔽p8|2N_{V}/|\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}|; that pseudo-unit claim is a claim on a fixed linear combination of committed columns, which the global proof tests like any other. The independent coefficients αk′\alpha^{\prime}_{k} and λt\lambda_{t} in 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}} make the batched codeword far from the code whenever one of its constituents is, except with the correlated-agreement error, which is included in ϵprox\epsilon_{\mathrm{prox}}.
