For η=0.01\eta=0.01, m=⌈ρ/(2​η)⌉=36m=\lceil\sqrt{\rho}/(2\eta)\rceil=36, and codewords of 2242^{24} symbols, correlated agreement over lines holds with error ϵline=(m+12)7​n2/(3​ρ3/2​|𝔽p8|)≈2−163.6\epsilon_{\mathrm{line}}=(m+\tfrac{1}{2})^{7}n^{2}/(3\rho^{3/2}|\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}|)\approx 2^{-163.6} for δ≤1−ρ−ρ/(2​m)\delta\leq 1-\sqrt{\rho}-\sqrt{\rho}/(2m) [BSCI+20, Thm. 5.1]. The batch draws an independent coefficient per column, so the combined words form an affine space. The proof of correlated agreement over affine spaces [BSCI+20, Thm. 1.6, Sec. 6.3] applies the line theorem as a black box and needs, besides, fewer than |𝔽p8||\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}}| codewords within distance δ\delta of a word, which holds in the Johnson regime; so it holds with the same error, and ϵprox=ϵline≈2−163.6\epsilon_{\mathrm{prox}}=\epsilon_{\mathrm{line}}\approx 2^{-163.6} per entry level (above 2−1592^{-159} after the union bound of condition 1), and the queries give 153⋅0.4797+30=103.4153\cdot 0.4797+30=103.4 bits.

8.3 Soundness

Theorem 8.4 (Soundness).

Model BLAKE3 as a random oracle. Let 𝗌𝗍\mathsf{st} be a statement whose CWC_{W} commits to a valid model (weights in [−127,127][-127,127] and embedding rows in AA, as produced by the program of Section 5.7), and such that no WW committed by CWC_{W} satisfies (𝗌𝗍,W)∈ℛ(\mathsf{st},W)\in\mathcal{R}. Then any prover that makes at most QQ random-oracle queries makes the Sable verifier accept 𝗌𝗍\mathsf{st} with probability at most Q⋅ϵrbr+O⁡(Q2/2256)Q\cdot\epsilon_{\mathrm{rbr}}+O(Q^{2}/2^{256}), where ϵrbr≤2−103.4\epsilon_{\mathrm{rbr}}\leq 2^{-103.4} is the maximum of the terms in Table 2. Here a query counts once per evaluation of the transcript hash, and the proofs of work make each attempt at the two challenges they precede cost 2302^{30} and 2112^{11} evaluations: without them the two tightest terms are ϵquery=(1/2+0.01)153=2−73.4\epsilon_{\mathrm{query}}=(\sqrt{1/2}+0.01)^{153}=2^{-73.4} and ϵLU=2−92.9\epsilon_{\mathrm{LU}}=2^{-92.9} per attempt.

Proof sketch.

We show that the underlying IOP has round-by-round soundness error ϵrbr\epsilon_{\mathrm{rbr}}; the theorem then follows from the analysis of the Fiat–Shamir transform for such IOPs [CCH+19, BSCS16], with the O⁡(Q2/2256)O(Q^{2}/2^{256}) term accounting for hash collisions in the Merkle trees (Lemma 8.2).

The state function of the round-by-round analysis is the following predicate. Call a partial transcript doomed if some claim it contains is false with respect to the committed oracles: a claim on a column’s multilinear extension, a sumcheck or GKR claim, a fraction sum, or a recorded opening claim. Every term of Table 2 is the probability that one challenge turns a doomed transcript into one that is not, so it is a per-round escape probability; none of them is a union bound over a whole proof. A 1×41\times 4K proof draws about 5.1×1055.1\times 10^{5} challenges (Table 11), and ϵrbr\epsilon_{\mathrm{rbr}} bounds the escape probability at each of them. In particular, the LogUp test is a single round for all chunks: ZZ and the coefficients β\beta are drawn once, after all multiplicities are committed, and a doomed transcript escapes only if the identity of a chunk that contains a bad lookup holds at the drawn point, which Lemma 8.1 bounds for that chunk. By Lemmas 6.1 and 6.2, if every constraint, static lookup, gather and output constraint holds for the committed assignment, then the assignment is the execution of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} on the committed weights, and (𝗌𝗍,W)∈ℛ(\mathsf{st},W)\in\mathcal{R}. Hence, for a false statement, the committed assignment violates at least one of them, and the statement checks of Section 7.7 reject any assignment that violates none. The first challenge that tests the violated item then makes the transcript doomed except with probability bounded by one term of the budget: Lemma 7.1 for constraints and leaf fractions, Lemmas 7.2 and 8.1 for lookups and gathers, Lemma 3.1 for each product and reduction sumcheck, and the zerocheck bound for the output constraints. Each later round keeps a doomed transcript doomed except with probability at most the corresponding per-round term, since a false claim entering a sumcheck round yields a false claim leaving it unless the verifier’s challenge hits a root of a nonzero polynomial of the stated degree. At the end, a doomed transcript contains a false claim on a committed column, which the global evaluation proof rejects except with the probability of Lemma 8.3. ∎

Weight binding.

CWC_{W} is the digest of the weight units’ caps, so by Lemma 8.2 a proof that verifies against CWC_{W} is bound to one committed weight assignment. The proof does not check the ranges of the committed weights; they are a property of CWC_{W}, established by whoever computes it. For open weights, anyone recomputes CWC_{W} from the published checkpoint and quantization program, which also establishes the ranges. For closed weights the party that computes CWC_{W} is the one the verifier distrusts, and with out-of-range weights Lemmas 6.1 and 6.2 no longer hold; a one-time range proof of the committed weights per model release (one lookup per weight, about 3.3×10103.3\times 10^{10} lookups, a small fraction of one 16K proof’s 7.2×10117.2\times 10^{11}) would remove the assumption, and we have not built it.

What is not claimed.

The main proof is not zero-knowledge: the opened columns and claimed evaluations reveal information about the trace and about the weights. The weight codewords are fixed and every proof opens them at fresh positions, so about 1.9×1041.9\times 10^{4} proofs reveal enough codeword symbols to recover every weight column by linear algebra (Section 4); the system as built is for open-weight models. The statement concerns F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}: a sequence produced by other kernels will in general not satisfy ℛ\mathcal{R}, because one changed rounding decision changes every later token. Tokens injected by the server after the prompt (tool outputs, retrieved documents) are part of xx only if the client can check their provenance.

9 A single-GPU prover

The prover is written in Python on top of PyTorch, with CUDA kernels compiled at run time by NVRTC. Python orchestrates the protocol, and all arithmetic on witness-sized data runs on the GPU. This section describes the techniques that matter for its speed; Section 11.6 measures them.

9.1 Memory: streaming and recomputation

The witness of a 16,384-token proof is several terabytes, so no pass keeps it. The commit pass stores only the residual stream at layer boundaries (S⋅dS\cdot d values of 32 and 8 bits per layer, in pinned host memory). Each later phase that needs a layer’s witness (the prove pass and the query phase) recomputes it from the stored boundary with the same integer kernels as the forward pass, about 4242 ms per layer at 4,096 tokens. The per-layer reduction of Section 7.5 exists to keep this count at three builds per layer (commit, prove, query): without it, the global evaluation proof needed two more full passes over every layer, about 25%25\% of the proving time at every shape. Codewords are never stored either: the commit pass hashes them as it encodes, and the global evaluation proof re-encodes the combined columns. Peak GPU memory is 3737 GiB for one 4,096-token sequence and 7272 GiB for one 16,384-token sequence. Peak host memory is 100100 and 174174 GiB; the model’s 8-bit weights, kept in host memory and streamed to the GPU layer by layer, take about 3333 GiB of it, and the boundaries and the pinned pool of the per-layer reduction most of the rest.

9.2 Generated sumcheck kernels

Every domain defines a polynomial program, the bracket of (1), over its half-columns. The prover turns each program into a CUDA kernel that computes one round of the sumcheck. Each thread handles pairs of rows, evaluates the program at the round’s interpolation points {0,2,…,d}\{0,2,\ldots,d\}, and reduces the results across the grid. Coefficients that depend on challenges are kernel arguments read from shared memory, and format constants that differ per layer come from a device buffer, so one compiled kernel serves every layer of a model. Large programs (the MLP domain has dozens of columns and degree 10) use 224 to 255 registers per thread, and their rounds are limited by instruction latency while memory bandwidth stays far from saturated. Moving the extension-field coefficients from registers to shared memory reduced spilling and cut the GPU time of a layer by 3.6%3.6\%.

Base-field first rounds.

All committed values are base-field integers. The first round of every sumcheck reads base-field tables and evaluates the program with base-field arithmetic where its coefficients allow; the second round reads the base table again and folds it twice, with the first two challenges, before writing the quarter-size extension table that the third round reads. The more aggressive small-value algorithms of [BDT24, DDB+26] expand rounds 2 and 3 over Lagrange nodes and need the program’s coefficients in the base field. Ours are extension elements (challenge-weighted combinations of constraints and lookups), so those algorithms would roughly double the evaluations per pair; our estimate of their gain on top of the current scheme is about 1%1\% of the proof.

Lookup leaves.

A lookup with numerator one contributes a⁡(q0+q1)+a​λ​q0​q1a(q_{0}+q_{1})+a\lambda q_{0}q_{1} to (1). We evaluate it as a​λ​(q0+μ)​(q1+μ)−a​μa\lambda(q_{0}+\mu)(q_{1}+\mu)-a\mu with μ=1/λ\mu=1/\lambda, folding a​λa\lambda into the coefficients of q0q_{0}. This halves the extension multiplications per lookup in the compute-bound first round.

GKR rounds.

Large GKR rounds run at 83 to 88% of the GPU’s memory bandwidth and are close to the roofline for reading, folding and writing the layer. Small rounds (at most 2152^{15} pairs) are latency-bound; we spread their (pair, lookup) work items over all blocks of the grid instead of looping over lookups in one thread, which cut the GPU time of a layer from 1.011.01 to 0.900.90 s at 4,096 tokens.

9.3 Field arithmetic

Base-field products use Barrett reduction of 62-bit products. For 𝔽p4=𝔽p​[Y]/(Y4−3)\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}=\mathbb{F}_{p}[Y]/(Y^{4}-3) we use the schoolbook product with the factor 33 folded into one operand: each output coordinate is a sum of four products below p2p^{2}, so the sum is below 4​p2<2644p^{2}<2^{64} and needs a single reduction. This raised the measured throughput of 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} multiplications from 255255 to 371371 billion per second on our GPU (one reduction per coordinate against Karatsuba over 𝔽p2\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}} with six reductions), and cut the MLP domain’s sumcheck from 40.840.8 to 36.636.6 ms. An instruction count had predicted no gain, because the 64-bit Barrett reduction costs more than the multiplications it saves. 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}} uses Karatsuba over the faster 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}}; a delayed reduction does not fit in 64 bits there, since eight products would be summed per coordinate. The same delayed reduction in the linear-combination kernel of the commitment brings it to the memory bandwidth limit (4.79→3.834.79\to 3.83 ms for 128 columns of 2232^{23}).

Opening kernels.

A unit opening needs, for every column, its value at the reduced point ρ\rho, and the combination ∑kαk′​fk\sum_{k}\alpha^{\prime}_{k}f_{k} folded at the high coordinates of ρ\rho. Computing the values as dot products with a full eq⁡(ρ,⋅)\mathrm{eq}(\rho,\cdot) table reads 16 bytes of table per 4-byte column element. One kernel instead folds every column at the high coordinates with a table of at most 2122^{12} entries, reading each column once; the values and the folded combination follow from the folded vectors of at most 2112^{11} entries. This cut the proving time of 8 layers by 1.6%1.6\% at 4,096 tokens and 2.4%2.4\% at 16,384 tokens.

9.4 A device-resident transcript

A sumcheck round needs the transcript between two kernels: absorb the round message, squeeze the challenge, fold. With the transcript on the host, each round costs a device-to-host copy and a synchronization, and the prove pass of one layer at 4,096 tokens has several thousand rounds. Sable keeps the transcript state (Section 3.5) on the GPU. The last block of each round kernel absorbs the round message and derives the challenge. One warp performs each compression, with lane j<16j<16 holding word jj of the block, so that a block is filled in one step and the compression reads its message through warp shuffles. This brought a round’s transcript step from 25.925.9 to 8.8​μ8.8\,\mus. The device transcript absorbs exactly the bytes the host transcript would and samples challenges by the same rejection loop, so proofs are byte-identical either way, which the tests check; the verifier always uses the host implementation.

The prover never needs the values of the claims it produces, since they matter only to the verifier’s checks. In the prove pass, claimed values, points and coefficients therefore stay on the device as lazy values, and the commitment’s openings run on the same device transcript. A whole layer’s prove pass then runs without a host synchronization.

9.5 Graph replay

The prove passes of the middle layers launch the same kernels with the same shapes; only the data differs. Sable captures the prove pass of layer L−2L-2 once as a CUDA graph and replays it for layers L−3,…,1L-3,\ldots,1. Before each replay, the inputs are written into fixed buffers: the layer’s weights, its stored boundary, its format constants, and the incoming claims. After each replay, the outputs are relabeled: claims on layer l−1l-1 with shifted challenge indices, the opening states, and the transcript messages. Three rules keep the replay identical to a plain run. Every constant that depends on the layer index is read from a device buffer. The transcript absorbs the layer index once at the start of the layer, and every later label omits it. Claims that a layer makes on the fixed units are replayed per layer from a template. The proof is byte-identical to that of the plain prover. At 4,096 tokens, replay brings a 64-layer proof from 133133 to 106106 s, 0.430.43 s per replayed layer; at 16,384 tokens the prover is GPU-bound and the gain is 1%1\%. The gain is larger than the 0.270.27 s of host-side Python time per layer that we measured on 8-layer proofs without replay; we did not isolate the remainder, which may come from the order of kernels in the captured graph.

9.6 Other kernels

Reed–Solomon encoding uses a radix-22 NTT in two passes for codewords up to 2242^{24} symbols: the last pass covers up to 13 contiguous bits, the others up to 10, in tiles of 8,192 symbols. Encoding 26 codewords of 2242^{24} symbols takes 6.26.2 ms. Softmax multiplicities come from a histogram that the attention witness kernel accumulates in shared memory, which avoids rebuilding the tile domain’s columns and saved 3%3\% at 16,384 tokens. Multiplicity columns stay on the host as bytes with a sparse list of larger entries, and are compressed on a side stream.

10 Toward recursive compression

A proof of 134.8 MiB is acceptable for an auditor who verifies it once, but too large to return with every response or to publish. The intended form for every client is a recursive proof: a proof, in the same proof system, that the Sable verifier accepts the main proof. Its outer layers would be zero-knowledge, and the final layer would use a low-rate code for a short proof. Its cost is set by what the main verifier computes, so this section first reduces the verifier’s work and then gives the first circuit component, BLAKE3.

10.1 What the verifier computes

We count the verifier’s operations by instrumenting the reference verifier. For the full 64-layer model on one 4,096-token sequence, the verifier originally performed 17.817.8 million BLAKE3 compressions: 10.610.6 million in the transcript and 7.27.2 million for Merkle leaves and paths. It also performed about 1111 million 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} multiplications and, through the public columns it evaluated by folding, about 4.7×1094.7\times 10^{9} folded elements per proof. A recursive circuit that pays about 40964096 trace cells per compression and 1616 per extension operation would cost more than a third of the main proof. We removed this work in the following steps, each a protocol change with its own tests.

  1. 1.

    Closed-form public columns. Every structured public column has an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) closed-form multilinear extension: index columns ii and (i≫s)≪s(i\gg s)\ll s are ∑j2j​xj\sum_{j}2^{j}x_{j} over the kept bits, the causal tile mask [c≤r][c\leq r] is a comparator evaluated from the top bit, and the vocabulary indicators [v<yt][v<y_{t}], [v=yt][v=y_{t}] and one-hots are comparators against the constant yty_{t}, weighted by eq\mathrm{eq} over the rows.

  2. 2.

    Committed fixed tables. The 2262^{26}-row table 𝒯\mathcal{T} and the RoPE tables are committed once per model and shape as fixed units. The prover sends the table’s evaluations, which become claims on these units, and the verifier compares their caps with precomputed digests. On a small test model this cut the verifier’s folded elements from 4.7×1094.7\times 10^{9} to 3×1043\times 10^{4}.

  3. 3.

    Recorded final openings. After the query positions are drawn, nothing else is drawn, so absorbing the leaf values and paths into the transcript binds nothing; they are now recorded in the proof without being hashed. For one layer this reduced the absorbed bytes from 11.011.0 to 1.51.5 MiB.

  4. 4.

    Fewer, wider columns. Every query opens every column, so the number of columns, more than the number of committed elements, sets the leaf hashing. Tensors with few small blocks share columns, with padding allowed up to 2202^{20} elements; the attention probabilities are packed into wide columns after the prover sends each block’s value at the shared point; the weights are packed flat. Columns fell from 84.884.8K to 32.632.6K at a cost of 2.5%2.5\% more committed elements.

  5. 5.

    Shared Merkle paths. A layer’s units share trees, first one per class and then one mixed-height tree per layer (Section 7.5).

Table 3 gives the totals. The remaining transcript work is driven by challenges: 506506K challenges, mostly GKR rounds, of which a tree of depth nn has n⁡(n+1)/2n(n+1)/2, each cost one output compression, and their round messages and re-absorbed outputs make up most of the 1.211.21M absorbing compressions. The remaining Merkle work is mostly leaf hashing. The final verifier also performs 11.011.0 million 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} multiplications, 4.64.6 million 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} additions, 0.260.26 million 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} inversions and 0.220.22 million 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}} multiplications. Under the cell counts above, layer 1 of the recursion would have about 1.8×10101.8\times 10^{10} cells, which the cost model of Section 11.5 prices at about 10%10\% of the main proof. The Python reference verifier takes 9494 s for this proof (Section 11).

10.2 BLAKE3 in a domain

The recursive verifier is a computation over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} and its extensions plus BLAKE3, and we prove it with the same domains, lookups and commitment as the main proof. BLAKE3’s compression function applies the function GG 56 times (7 rounds of 8 calls) to a state of sixteen 32-bit words, with two message words per call:

s1\displaystyle s_{1} =a+b+mx,\displaystyle=a+b+m_{x}, x1\displaystyle x_{1} =d⊕s1,\displaystyle=d\oplus s_{1}, d1\displaystyle d_{1} =x1⋙16,\displaystyle=x_{1}\ggg 16,
s2\displaystyle s_{2} =c+d1,\displaystyle=c+d_{1}, x2\displaystyle x_{2} =b⊕s2,\displaystyle=b\oplus s_{2}, b1\displaystyle b_{1} =x2⋙12,\displaystyle=x_{2}\ggg 12,
s3\displaystyle s_{3} =s1+b1+my,\displaystyle=s_{1}+b_{1}+m_{y}, x3\displaystyle x_{3} =d1⊕s3,\displaystyle=d_{1}\oplus s_{3}, d2\displaystyle d_{2} =x3⋙8,\displaystyle=x_{3}\ggg 8,
s4\displaystyle s_{4} =s2+d2,\displaystyle=s_{2}+d_{2}, x4\displaystyle x_{4} =b1⊕s4,\displaystyle=b_{1}\oplus s_{4}, b2\displaystyle b_{2} =x4⋙7,\displaystyle=x_{4}\ggg 7,

with outputs (s3,b2,s4,d2)(s_{3},b_{2},s_{4},d_{2}) and additions modulo 2322^{32}.

The G row.

A 32-bit word does not fit in 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, so every word is held as four bytes. One domain row proves one call of GG with 80 columns: the bytes of the inputs a,b,c,d,mx,mya,b,c,d,m_{x},m_{y}; the bytes of s1,…,s4s_{1},\ldots,s_{4}; the carries ki,1..4k_{i,1..4} of the four additions; the bytes of x1x_{1} and x3x_{3}; the nibbles hj,ljh_{j},l_{j} of the bytes of x2x_{2}; and the top bit tjt_{j} and low seven bits rjr_{j} of the bytes of x4x_{4}.

  • •

    Additions: per byte jj, a linear constraint such as aj+bj+mx,j+k1,j−s1,j−256​k1,j+1=0a_{j}+b_{j}+m_{x,j}+k_{1,j}-s_{1,j}-256\,k_{1,j+1}=0 (with ki,0=0k_{i,0}=0), and the carry range k​(k−1)​(k−2)=0k(k-1)(k-2)=0 for the three-operand additions and k⁡(k−1)=0k(k-1)=0 for the others.

  • •

    XOR: lookups into three tables of 2162^{16} rows: (u,v,u⊕v)(u,v,u\oplus v) for x1x_{1} and x3x_{3}; (u,v,(u⊕v)≫4,(u⊕v)&15)(u,v,(u\oplus v)\gg 4,(u\oplus v)\mathbin{\&}15) for x2x_{2}; and (u,v,(u⊕v)≫7,(u⊕v)&127)(u,v,(u\oplus v)\gg 7,(u\oplus v)\mathbin{\&}127) for x4x_{4}. The tables contain only bytes, so these lookups also bound every byte they read.

  • •

    Rotations: by 16 and 8 bits they permute bytes: d1,j=x1,(j+2)mod4d_{1,j}=x_{1,(j+2)\bmod 4}, d2,j=x3,(j+1)mod4d_{2,j}=x_{3,(j+1)\bmod 4}. By 12 and 7 bits they recombine the split parts: b1,j=h(j+1)mod4+16​l(j+2)mod4b_{1,j}=h_{(j+1)\bmod 4}+16\,l_{(j+2)\bmod 4} and b2,j=2​r(j+1)mod4+tjb_{2,j}=2\,r_{(j+1)\bmod 4}+t_{j}.

A row has 32 constraints of degree at most 3 and 16 lookups. All sums are below 2112^{11}, so the constraints are wrap-free.

Wiring.

The rows are connected by a LogUp memory (Figure 4). Each word is a tuple (𝖬𝖤𝖬,𝑖𝑑,b0,b1,b2,b3)(\mathsf{MEM},\mathit{id},b_{0},b_{1},b_{2},b_{3}) in a dynamic set. The row that produces a word writes it with numerator −μ-\mu, where μ\mu is the number of times the word will be read, and each consumer reads it with numerator +1+1. For compression cc, state slot ss at version vv has 𝑖𝑑=512​c+16​s+v\mathit{id}=512c+16s+v; each half-round writes every slot once, so versions run from 00 to 1414. Message word ww has 𝑖𝑑=512​c+256+w\mathit{id}=512c+256+w and is read seven times. G rows read their six inputs and write their four outputs. Input rows write the initial state (chaining value, IV, counter, block length, flags) at version 00 and the message words with multiplicity 77. Output rows read slots ii and i+8i+8 at version 1414, XOR them, and write output word ii under a separate tag. The ids come from public columns, a per-compression base 512​c512c and a per-position offset shared by all compressions, both with closed forms, and the multiplicities are constants of the layout, so no multiplicity column is committed. Bytes written to the memory are bounded by the XOR lookups (G rows) or by range lookups (input rows), so reads need no range checks of their own.

Lemma 10.1 (Memory).

Suppose the ids written by the layout are distinct, every id is written once with multiplicity equal to the number of reads of that id in the layout, and all multiplicities are below pp. If the memory set’s fractions sum to zero as a rational function, then every read returns the bytes written under its id.

Proof.

Group the tuples by id. By Lemma 3.2 applied to the multiset of reads and the written tuples with their multiplicities, the multiset of read tuples equals the multiset of written tuples, each counted with its multiplicity. Since each id is written exactly once, every read tuple with id ii must equal the unique written tuple with id ii, and the counts match by assumption on the layout. ∎

Together with the row constraints, Lemma 10.1 implies that the output rows hold the BLAKE3 compression of the input rows. We tested the gadget against a reference implementation and two forgeries: a forged XOR byte with every arithmetic constraint repaired, and a message word in the input rows that differs from the one the G rows read. Both are rejected.

Cost.

A compression has 64×80+32×4+8×12=5,34464\times 80+32\times 4+8\times 12=5{,}344 committed cells, 30%30\% above the 4,0964{,}096 of the design estimate. We measured the full cost of a block of compressions on our GPU: commitment of its trace, the domain proofs of its G, input, output and table rows, and the openings of its units at the domains’ points (the global evaluation proof, shared by all blocks of a recursion layer, is not included). A block of 2162^{16} compressions (2222^{22} G rows) takes 0.160.16 s, 2.4​μ2.4\,\mus per compression: 1313 ms of commitment, 0.130.13 s of domain proofs and 1515 ms of openings. A block of 2182^{18} compressions (2242^{24} rows) takes 0.330.33 s, 1.3​μ1.3\,\mus per compression, because the upper GKR layers are latency-bound and barely grow with the block. At that rate the 4.24.2 million compressions of a 64-layer 1×41\times 4K verifier cost about 5.55.5 s, 6%6\% of the main proof, and the 9.29.2 million of a 1616K verifier about 1212 s, 3%3\%. The extension-field arithmetic of the verifier (1111 to 1717 million 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} multiplications) is not yet a circuit and is not included.

10.3 What remains

The recursive layer also needs gadgets for 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} and 𝔽p8\mathbb{F}_{p^{8}} arithmetic, a recorder that turns a run of the verifier into the layer’s witness (with chaining between the transcript, Merkle and leaf compressions), segmentation into fixed-size circuits, outer layers, and a final layer at a low code rate. The outer layers must be zero-knowledge, which needs hiding commitments and masked sumcheck and GKR messages for multilinear arguments [CFS17, XZZ+19]; this mode is not yet built.

11 Evaluation

11.1 Setup

Hardware and software.

All measurements use one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (96 GB GDDR7, compute capability 12.0) in a host with an Intel Xeon 6776P (24 cores available) and 214 GB of memory. The code is that of the public release (https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable), whose README lists the command behind each table. Software: Linux 6.11, NVIDIA driver 580.159 with CUDA 13.0, PyTorch 2.14 and CuPy 14.2 (NVRTC). The GPU was shared with another user’s jobs; every reported run was taken while the GPU was otherwise idle, as checked before and after the run.

Model and workloads.

Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct quantized to F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} (Section 5.7), all 64 layers; Section 11.3 adds Qwen3-32B (64 layers) and Qwen3-30B-A3B (48 layers). Three shapes: one sequence of 4,096 tokens (1×41\times 4K), four sequences of 4,096 tokens in one proof (4×44\times 4K), and one sequence of 16,384 tokens (1616K). Each sequence consists of a prompt of uniformly random token ids followed by 16 greedily generated tokens, which the proof covers together with the stopping rule; the cost depends on the total length and hardly on the split between prompt and generation. The prover’s work does not depend on the token values, since every gadget commits and checks every row whatever its value.

What is timed.

Wall-clock time of the prover from the statement to the last proof message, with the weight commitment computed beforehand (it is a property of the model release, computed once) and all kernels compiled. The kernels are compiled at run time and cached on disk; with an empty cache, the first 1×41\times 4K proof took 1,5301{,}530 s against 9292 s for a second proof in the same process, so compilation is a one-time cost of about 24 minutes per machine and GPU type, which we exclude. The prover keeps a pool of pinned host memory for the per-layer reduction (Section 7.5); it is allocated by the first proof of a process, which also captures the CUDA graphs and is therefore slower (103103, 328328 and 427427 s at the three shapes). The end-to-end results (Tables 4 and 5) are the mean of three warm runs that follow such a warm-up run in the same process. Other numbers, measured during development to compare variants of the prover, are single warm runs; repeated warm runs of the same configuration differed by up to about 2%2\%. Runs use the protocol of Sections 7 and 8.

11.2 End-to-end proving

Table 4 gives the end-to-end results and Table 5 every timed run. The 4×44\times 4K proof covers four times the tokens of the 1×41\times 4K proof in 2.742.74 times the time: weights, the table side and the evaluation proof are shared, and the larger domains use the GPU better. The 1616K proof takes 1.571.57 times as long as 4×44\times 4K for the same number of tokens, because attention grows quadratically with the sequence length: a 1616K sequence has 44 times as many causal score entries as four sequences of 44K. Proving time per token is nearly the same at 1×41\times 4K and 1616K (22.622.6 and 24.324.3 ms): at 4K the prover is close to its fixed per-token cost, and attention catches up by 1616K. The prover’s work does not depend on the prompt: a 1×41\times 4K proof of a WikiText-2 prompt takes the same time as one of random ids (92.392.3 against 92.592.5 s), with the same 1.0765×10111.0765\times 10^{11} lookups. At temperature 1.01.0, the sampling gadget (Section 6.5) adds 304304 lookups and 0.080.08 MiB, its proving time is within the variation between processes (92.392.3 against 92.592.5 s), and the proof verifies. The proofs make 1.08×10111.08\times 10^{11}, 4.31×10114.31\times 10^{11} and 7.20×10117.20\times 10^{11} static lookups, in 103103, 416416 and 726726 chunks of at most 2302^{30}.

Before the proof-size reductions of Section 10, the same proofs took 101.3101.3, 298.1298.1 and 474.3474.3 s and were 360.0360.0, 468.0468.0 and 549.6549.6 MiB long. With the final layout and soundness bounds, and a global evaluation proof that rebuilt every layer’s witness in three passes, they took 108.2108.2, 304.7304.7 and 479.1479.1 s; the optimizations of Table 10 then brought them to the times of Table 4, mostly through the per-layer reduction, which removed two of the three rebuild passes.

Overhead and cost.

Our serving engine for F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} (Section 12) computes the same work as the 1×41\times 4K proof, prefill and 16 generated tokens, in 1.861.86 s (time to first token 1.301.30 s, then 37.437.4 ms per token), the 4×44\times 4K work in 5.605.60 s and the 1616K work in 9.609.60 s. A proof therefore takes 41 to 50 times the inference it attests. Against FP8 in SGLang, which prefills 4,096 tokens in 0.460.46 s and decodes 15 more in about 0.60.6 s, the factor is about 90. At a public on-demand price of 2.50 dollars per GPU-hour for this GPU [Cor26], a 1×41\times 4K proof costs 6.46.4 cents, a sequence in a 4×44\times 4K proof 4.44.4 cents, and a 1616K proof 2828 cents. Several sequences per proof amortize the shared work, but the GPU’s 96 GB bound the shapes. We probed larger ones with 4-layer proofs, whose peak GPU memory is set by one layer as in a 64-layer proof: a proof of eight 4K sequences runs out of GPU memory in the prove pass, and one of a 32K sequence in its first witness build.

Where the time goes.

We profiled 8-layer proofs with Nsight Systems, tracing the kernels inside replayed graphs, first in the configuration before the per-layer reduction. Per replayed layer, the prove pass keeps the GPU busy 94%94\%, 97%97\% and 97%97\% of the time at the three shapes (0.900.90, 2.632.63 and 4.224.22 s of span), so the prover is GPU-bound there. Over the whole 1616K proof, the prove pass took about 55%55\% of the time, the three rebuild passes at the end 26%26\% and the commit pass 16%16\%; the per-layer reduction removed most of the second item, and in the final prover the remaining query pass takes 1111, 3232 and 5353 s at the three shapes. Within the prove pass of one layer at 1×41\times 4K, sumcheck round kernels take 512512 ms: 4,6004{,}600 rounds below 30​μ30\,\mus cost 8080 ms in total, and 630630 rounds above 100​μ100\,\mus cost 400400 ms. By protocol step, the MLP domains take 133133 ms, the softmax tile domains 119119 ms, the unit openings’ point reductions 100100 ms, and data preparation outside sumchecks (witness, column packing, the reductions’ tables) 268268 ms. At 1616K the tile domains take 1.251.25 s of the prove pass per layer, close to the cost model’s charge (Section 11.5) for their 5.4×1095.4\times 10^{9} lookup leaves per layer. The large GKR rounds already run at 83 to 88% of memory bandwidth; the domain rounds are compute-bound (Section 9.2).

Table 6 gives the same breakdown for the final prover. The prove pass is 88%88\% to 96%96\% busy; the commit pass and the final passes, which are not replayed as graphs, 56%56\% to 87%87\%. In the final passes at 1616K, Reed–Solomon encoding takes 298298 ms per layer and leaf hashing 7171 ms, the rest being witness reconstruction and column packing; keeping the Merkle levels in host memory from the commit pass and encoding only the queried tiles saves about 1%1\% of the 1×41\times 4K proof, but the stored levels exceed the host memory of our machine at the larger shapes, so the final prover recomputes them. The proofs make 1.08×10111.08\times 10^{11}, 4.31×10114.31\times 10^{11} and 7.20×10117.20\times 10^{11} static lookups, in 103103, 416416 and 726726 chunks of at most 2302^{30}.

11.3 Proving Qwen3

Table 7 gives the end-to-end results for the two Qwen3 models, with the shapes, workloads and protocol of Table 4. Qwen3-32B has the depth and width of Qwen2.5-32B, but 64 query heads instead of 40, QK-norm, and a slightly narrower MLP. Its proofs make 1.39×10111.39\times 10^{11}, 5.56×10115.56\times 10^{11} and 1.02×10121.02\times 10^{12} static lookups, 1.291.29, 1.291.29 and 1.421.42 times those of Qwen2.5-32B, and take 1.321.32, 1.921.92 and 1.681.68 times as long. The gap is largest at the two larger shapes, where attention takes a larger share of the proof and where the prover runs without graph replay, because the captured graphs no longer fit in 96 GB beside the larger attention witness. Graph replay saved 4%4\% and 1%1\% of the Qwen2.5 proofs at these shapes (Table 10), so its absence explains little of the difference; the larger attention explains part of it, and at 4×44\times 4K we did not locate the rest.

Qwen3-30B-A3B has 48 layers of width 2,048, 32 query heads, and 128 experts of width 768 per layer, of which each token uses 8. The proof binds all 30.5×10930.5\times 10^{9} weights through the weight commitment but proves only the experts each token selects, so it makes 4.65×10104.65\times 10^{10}, 1.86×10111.86\times 10^{11} and 3.60×10113.60\times 10^{11} lookups, about a third of those of Qwen3-32B, and takes 84.784.7, 181.9181.9 and 265.7265.7 s. The 4×44\times 4K proof covers four times the tokens of the 1×41\times 4K proof in 2.152.15 times the time (2.742.74 for Qwen2.5-32B): the work on the weights is shared between the sequences, and it is a larger part of the proof when each token uses a tenth of them. The overhead factor of this model is lower because our serving engine decodes it in 201201 ms per token, five times the 3838 ms of Qwen3-32B: it runs the experts through the exact integer grouped product of the prover’s witness, which a decoding step of one token uses poorly. Against prefill alone, the 1×41\times 4K proof takes 4141 times the 2.062.06 s our engine needs to prefill 4,096 tokens.

On one CPU core, the verifier checks the six proofs in 20.220.2 to 55.855.8 s; on the GPU, run in a fresh process, it takes 21.421.4 to 53.153.1 s, no faster, since the GPU path runs the protocol logic in Python without the compiled core. For serving, our engine generates 512 tokens after a 4,096-token prompt at 26.626.6 tokens per second for Qwen3-32B and 5.05.0 for Qwen3-30B-A3B in a batch of one, and at 412412 and 131131 tokens per second in a batch of 32.

11.4 Comparison with prior systems

Table 8 normalizes proving time by model size and number of tokens. zkLLM [SLZ24] takes 30.230.2 ps per parameter and token for LLaMa-2-13B on an A100; Sable takes 0.480.48 to 0.750.75 ps on Qwen2.5-32B, 40 to 64 times less. Part of this factor is hardware: our GPU has 3.53.5 times as many CUDA cores as the A100, at a higher clock. The systems also prove different statements: zkLLM hides the weights and works over a pairing-friendly field with approximate non-linear functions, while Sable is not zero-knowledge and fixes every rounding of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}. FlashProve [Ant26] proves a much larger mixture of experts on an H100 with 24 CPU cores in 0.560.56 ps per active parameter and token, within the range of Sable’s dense proofs and 6 to 11 times less than Sable’s proofs of Qwen3-30B-A3B, whose cost per active parameter is high partly because attention and the commitment of all 30.5B weights do not shrink with the experts a token uses. FlashProve works at a context of 1,024 tokens, where attention is a small part of the work, and includes zero knowledge, which for Sable is future work. zkGPT [QSL+25] proves GPT-2 (124M parameters) in 21.821.8 s on a 16-core CPU and reports zkLLM at 15.815.8 s on the same model; it does not state the number of tokens, so we do not normalize it.

11.5 Comparison with the cost model

Before implementing the prover, we built a cost model that counts, for every gadget, the committed elements, lookup leaves and constraint terms per element of the trace, and prices them from hardware rates: 3.9×10−103.9\times 10^{-10} H100-seconds per committed element (0.6×0.6\times that at rate 1/21/2), 1.5×10−101.5\times 10^{-10} per lookup leaf, 5.5×10−115.5\times 10^{-11} per constraint term, with factors of 0.70.7 and 0.50.5 for base-field first rounds, plus the forward passes and the weight opening. To price the same work on our GPU, a second model splits each unit cost into the resources it uses (32-bit multiplies, other integer operations, DRAM traffic, INT8 tensor operations and host transfers), from operation and byte counts of the algorithm behind it, and scales each share by the ratio of the two GPUs’ throughputs for that resource, from published architecture figures. It uses no measurement of the prover. Its central scenario takes the RTX PRO 6000 at its boost clock with 96 of its 128 integer lanes per multiprocessor effective for the operation mix and its full memory bandwidth; a low and a high scenario bracket the clock, the integer issue rate and the effective bandwidth. Per unit, commitment then costs 0.870.87 times its H100 time, a lookup leaf 1.031.03 times and a constraint term 1.101.10 times, so the model prices our GPU at about one H100. Table 9 compares its predictions with the measurements.

The model’s count of committed trace elements is within 5%5\% of the implementation’s, padding included, so the gadget accounting is accurate. The prover takes 2.452.45, 1.731.73 and 1.561.56 times the central prediction, falling as the shapes grow; at 1×41\times 4K this is outside the model’s stated factor of two, and against the low scenario the ratios are 2.102.10, 1.481.48 and 1.341.34. At 1×41\times 4K the prover is partly limited by latency: it runs about 3,800 single-block sumcheck rounds per layer, each taking 1212 to 18​μ18\,\mus of kernel time regardless of its size, most of it the round’s transcript step, and the GPU idles between domains while the host computes small claims. At 1616K the remaining gap is concentrated in attention: the final sumcheck of a softmax tile domain runs compute-bound at one thread block per multiprocessor (its kernels need over 200 registers per thread), and field additions with their conditional subtractions are about half of its instructions, which the model’s per-term multiplication counts do not capture. The model charges fixed costs per element and has no term for latency, which is where the small shape loses most. Its remaining uncertainty is the integer issue rate of the RTX PRO 6000, which the scenarios bracket; the gap at 1616K is larger than that range.

11.6 Engineering ablations

Table 10 lists the measured effect of the main optimizations. Removing host round trips mattered most: implicit synchronizations (pageable copies, data-dependent output sizes, scalar reads), the host transcript, and the Python overhead of launching each layer’s work. They took an 8-layer 1×41\times 4K proof from about 2323 s to 1616 s, and with graph replay the 64-layer 1×41\times 4K proof went from 134134 s to 101101 s. Kernel-level changes then brought the GPU time of a replayed layer from 1.011.01 to 0.830.83 s.

Several attempts gave no gain and were reverted: a register cap on the round kernels (spills doubled), splitting the off-diagonal attention tiles into a separate lower-degree domain (the extra GKR and reductions cost more than the lower degree saved), a fused single-kernel sumcheck tail, graph replay of the commitment passes (already GPU-bound), splitting each (pair, point) of the round polynomial into its own thread (40.8→52.640.8\to 52.6 ms for the MLP domain), compiling the witness with torch.compile (faster witness alone, 42.6→34.242.6\to 34.2 ms per layer, but slower proofs and 9.59.5 GiB more memory), and keeping the commitment’s combined column to skip one witness rebuild (1.3 to 4.4 GiB per layer).

Comparison with an external library.

We compared three kernels with the SP1-GPU library (version 6.9.0, which builds on sppark) on the same GPU and shapes. A coset low-degree extension of 26 columns from 2232^{23} to 2242^{24} took 10.210.2 ms there and 6.16.1 ms in Sable. A product sumcheck over 2242^{24} took 1.171.17 ms there (kernels only, no transcript) and 1.501.50 ms in Sable (with the device transcript). A LogUp-GKR layer took 3.543.54 ms there against 3.283.28 ms for 2242^{24} leaves, and 0.270.27 against 0.610.61 ms for 2202^{20}, where our per-round transcript dominates. No library we tested would make the prover as a whole faster.

11.7 Proof size and verification

For the final prover the proofs are 134.8134.8, 239.0239.0 and 345.7345.7 MiB at the three shapes (1.371.37, 1.781.78 and 1.861.86 million messages). At 1×41\times 4K, the leaf data of the query openings (32.632.6K columns at 4 positions for 153 queries) is 7676 MiB; Merkle paths, unit openings and the round messages of sumchecks and GKR make up the rest. The Python reference verifier, single-threaded with NumPy, takes 9494, 129129 and 145145 s; its time is dominated by interpreter overhead. Table 11 counts its operations. Verification grows slowly with the shape: from 1×41\times 4K to 1616K the trace grows 5.4×5.4\times, the BLAKE3 work 2.2×2.2\times and the 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} multiplications 1.5×1.5\times.

The reference verifier also runs on the host alone with a compiled core: the sumcheck and LogUp-GKR verifiers, equality tables, multilinear extensions and the product checks of the domain programs run in C++ on the transcript state and the proof’s messages, while the protocol logic (claim routing, opening bookkeeping) stays in Python. On one core of a Xeon 6776P, with no GPU, it verifies the three proofs in 18.818.8, 26.826.8 and 40.240.2 s, of which 1.31.3, 3.53.5 and 10.210.2 s are spent in the compiled core. The remainder is interpreter work on 1.41.4 to 1.91.9 million messages and the leaf hashing of the query openings through a Python binding, which a verifier compiled as a whole would remove. Its operation counts (Table 11) at single-core rates of a few hundred nanoseconds per BLAKE3 compression and tens of nanoseconds per 𝔽p4\mathbb{F}_{p^{4}} multiplication put such a verifier at a few seconds per proof.

11.8 Accuracy of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}

F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is a different function from the BF16 model, and its accuracy determines whether a deployment can serve it. We compare it with BF16 Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct and with two deployed 8-bit quantizations of the same checkpoint, simulated by quantizing and dequantizing in BF16: FP8 (E4M3, per-tensor scales, activations quantized dynamically) and SmoothQuant W8A8 INT8 [XLS+23] (smoothing strength 0.50.5 calibrated on 32,768 tokens of WikiText-2 training text, per-channel weights, per-token activations). F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is evaluated with an engine that computes the same integer function as the prover’s witness generator, vectorized over heads and sequences, and that we checked to produce identical logits and greedy tokens. WikiText-2 (raw) is tokenized as one string and cut into 145 non-overlapping windows of 2,048 tokens covering the whole test split, each evaluated from its first token (296,815 predictions); MMLU uses the 5-shot prompt of the original benchmark on all 14,042 test questions, scoring the answer letter with the largest logit; GSM8K uses the first 8 training problems with their worked answers as 8-shot prompt, greedy decoding of at most 256 tokens, and exact match of the final number on all 1,319 test problems. Intervals are 95% percentile intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of the WikiText-2 windows; since all variants see the same windows, differences between two variants are resampled jointly (paired), which gives much narrower intervals than those of single perplexities.

Table 12 gives the results. F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} loses more next-token accuracy than the deployed 8-bit schemes: its perplexity is 8.3%8.3\% above BF16’s, against 0.7%0.7\% and 1.6%1.6\% for FP8 and INT8, and its greedy token differs from BF16’s at 13.7%13.7\% of the positions. On MMLU, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is 1.41.4 points below BF16 (81.8%81.8\% against 83.2%83.2\%; 82.7%82.7\% against 84.2%84.2\% averaged over subjects), where FP8 and INT8 lose at most 0.20.2; on GSM8K, where answers depend on a chain of greedy decisions, it is 0.60.6 points below BF16, against 0.20.2 and 0.40.4 for FP8 and INT8. The left-shift regime of Remark 6.3 is common on real inputs: over the first 16 WikiText-2 windows, 4.1%4.1\% of the rows of the attention output and down projections have a shift k≤0k\leq 0, and 1.7%1.7\% a true left shift (down to k=−8k=-8); the logits never do. Honest proofs therefore exercise the input bound of Section 6.2.

Where the accuracy goes.

To find which of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}’s integer steps cost accuracy, we evaluated variants of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} that each make one step more precise and keep the weights, the calibration and every other step (Table 13): a float softmax computes the attention probabilities and their normalization in double precision from the same integer scores, instead of as 10-bit values with 16-bit denominator mantissas; 12-bit queries and keys shift by 4 bits less in the 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪𝖲\mathsf{ShiftQ8S} that produces them and saturate at 16⋅12716\cdot 127, with RoPE and the scores kept at this precision and the softmax scale divided by 282^{8}; a SiLU with 4 more bits evaluates SiLU in double precision on the same integer input and rounds it with 4 more fractional bits; a 16-bit up projection rounds the up projection to 16 bits instead of 8. In the last two, the shift after the gate product grows by the added bits. We also rebuilt F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} with the same program calibrated on 8 windows of 1,024 tokens from the WikiText-2 training split, instead of our technical text.

Only the queries and keys matter: with 12 bits they remove 37%37\% of the gap to BF16 and raise agreement to 88.6%88.6\%. The other three changes each move perplexity by less than 3%3\% of the gap, and all four together do no better than the queries and keys alone. Recalibrating on WikiText-2 text changes nothing, so the choice of calibration text does not explain the gap. The remaining 63%63\% lies in steps we did not vary; the 8-bit activations entering every projection and the 8-bit values VV are the obvious candidates.

The variants are not provable as they stand, because the extra bits break bounds of the constraint system. 12-bit queries and keys make scores reach 2302^{30}, far outside the 2232^{23}-entry exponential table, so a provable version would round each score by a shift before the table lookup, adding committed values and lookups to every causal score entry; 16-bit probabilities would make a P​VPV block sum reach 2352^{35}, above pp, and would need each probability committed as two 8-bit limbs. The cost model of Section 11.5 puts the first change at 1.301.30 times the proving time at 4K and 1.681.68 times at 1616K, the second at 1.151.15 and 1.351.35 times, and both at 1.451.45 and 2.022.02 times: precision is bought where the proof is already most expensive. Since the float softmax does not improve accuracy, only the first is worth building.

Qwen3.

Table 14 repeats the comparison for the two Qwen3 models of Section 5.6, with the same WikiText-2 windows and MMLU prompts. For GSM8K we raise the generation limit to 1,024 tokens for every variant of these models. The Qwen3 checkpoints are hybrid reasoning releases, and under a few-shot prompt without a chat template they sometimes open an answer in a step-by-step style (“Okay, let’s see…”) that runs past 256 tokens before its final number; at that limit the score would mostly count how often a variant switches style. Generation stops after the first complete final answer (#### N followed by a non-digit), which cannot change the extracted answer, since scoring reads the first such marker. F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is served by the engine of Section 12 with continuous batching, which computes each sequence exactly as it would alone.

On WikiText-2, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is 6.6%6.6\% above BF16 in perplexity on Qwen3-32B and 1.9%1.9\% on Qwen3-30B-A3B, and its greedy token agrees with BF16’s at 82.4%82.4\% and 88.7%88.7\% of the positions. The split of the score exponent between queries and keys (Section 5.7) accounts for much of this: the same models calibrated with all of the slack given to the keys are 8.6%8.6\% and 4.1%4.1\% above BF16, with agreement 79.3%79.3\% and 85.3%85.3\%, so the split removes 23%23\% (1919 to 2626) and 53%53\% (4646 to 6060) of the excess log perplexity, at no cost in the proof. On MMLU, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is 1.41.4 points below BF16 on Qwen3-32B and 1.61.6 on Qwen3-30B-A3B; the split gained 2.62.6 and 3.03.0 points (McNemar z=8.9z=8.9 and 10.310.3). On GSM8K it is 1.71.7 and 1.41.4 points below BF16, with 5454 against 3131 and 5050 against 3232 problems solved by only one of the two (McNemar z=−2.5z=-2.5 and −2.0-2.0); FP8 and SmoothQuant INT8 differ from BF16 by at most 0.50.5 points (|z|≤1.2|z|\leq 1.2).

The losses on the tasks are larger than on Qwen2.5 for two reasons that perplexity does not show. First, Qwen3 is less certain of its MMLU answers: on a subsample of every seventh question, measured on models calibrated with all of the slack given to the keys, the median margin between BF16’s best and second answer logit is 5.65.6 and 5.85.8 nats for Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-30B-A3B against 8.38.3 for Qwen2.5, while F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}’s error on that margin is 1.81.8 to 2.32.3 nats on all three models, so errors of the same size flip more answers. Applying the Qwen3 flip rate per margin to Qwen2.5’s margins accounts for about 85%85\% of the excess flips of Qwen3-30B-A3B and 60%60\% of those of Qwen3-32B. Second, on GSM8K the loss of Qwen3-32B is mostly a change of style: 527527 of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}’s 1,319 answers open in the step-by-step style, against 9292 for BF16, 4343 for FP8 and 324324 for SmoothQuant INT8. In every variant, answers in that style are right less often (89.2%89.2\% of them for F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}, 84.8%84.8\% for BF16) than direct answers, of which F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} gets 94.2%94.2\% right and BF16 94.6%94.6\%. Qwen3-30B-A3B never switches style under this prompt.

We repeated the attribution of Section 11.8 on both Qwen3 models over the first 24 WikiText-2 windows, with paired intervals (Table 15). On Qwen3-30B-A3B, 12-bit queries and keys remove all of the remaining gap and more (145%145\%, 119119 to 186186); every other step, including the router in floating point and an exact merge of the experts, is within noise of zero, except the float softmax, which makes the gap larger. On Qwen3-32B the input of the down projection matters most: leaving it unrounded removes 57%57\% (4747 to 6767), and rounding it to 9 bits instead of 8 removes 46%46\% (3333 to 5757); 12-bit queries and keys remove 21%21\%, an unrounded MLP input 12%12\%, and a float QK-norm, a float softmax or a SiLU with 4 more bits nothing distinguishable from zero. Smoothing the down input with power-of-two channel scales, which is provable, makes the gap several times larger.

The 9-bit down input is provable with the existing gadgets: 𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝖺𝗇𝗍𝟪\mathsf{Requant8} with bound 255 and the down projection’s 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖱𝗈𝗎𝗇𝖽\mathsf{ShiftRound} stay wrap-free while dff⋅127⋅255+230+223<pd_{\mathrm{ff}}\cdot 127\cdot 255+2^{30}+2^{23}<p, which holds for Qwen3-32B. We did not adopt it: on the model calibrated without the split, and with GSM8K generations limited to 256 tokens, it improved perplexity and MMLU but lowered GSM8K, a drop we could not separate from the change of style above. 12-bit queries and keys need the score rounding of Section 11.8; by the cost model they multiply the proving time of Qwen3-32B by 1.391.39 at 4K and 1.781.78 at 16K.

11.9 Where F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is undefined

We ran F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} with the three conditions of Section 5.7 recorded instead of enforced: a SiLU input |c|>214|c|>2^{14} or a gate shift outside [1,15][1,15]; an attention-output or down-projection shift outside [−16,24][-16,24]; and a left-shifted output outside AA. The scan runs the prefill of the evaluation engine, so it covers every prompt position and no generated one. Table 16 lists the inputs: every position of the WikiText-2 test split, all GSM8K prompts and 2,000 random MMLU prompts (3.45 million tokens of real text), and 160 adversarial sequences of 4,096 tokens.

For the Qwen3 models, the scan uses the serving engine (Section 12), which evaluates every condition of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}, including the QK-norm and router shifts, and flags each sequence that reaches one; we also ran every vocabulary token as a one-token prompt. No input reached any condition, so the honest prover would not have aborted on any of them. Without the row clamps of Section 5.6, 7 first tokens of Qwen3-32B and 2 of Qwen3-30B-A3B left the domain, all of them rare tokens whose first-position residual has a very small norm; the clamps define these rows and change no other row: on both models calibrated without the split, WikiText-2 predictions and GSM8K answers were identical with and without them. Calibration leaves margin: the SiLU range, for instance, is set 25%25\% above the largest gate input seen. This does not show that no input reaches a condition: an adversary who knows the weights could search for one, and a server could then refuse it. For open weights, the client can confirm such a refusal by evaluating F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} itself (Section 4).

11.10 Correctness and soundness testing

The test suite runs every protocol step on a small model with the shape of Qwen2 (two layers, width 256, four query and two key-value heads). Besides honest proofs, it checks rejection in five ways. Every message of a proof is corrupted in turn, and each corrupted proof must be rejected. A proof made with different weights must not verify against CWC_{W}. A proof whose sampled tokens do not follow from the seed must be rejected at temperature θ>0\theta>0. Targeted forgeries of the final openings (25 messages and 9 oracle elements) must be rejected. Forgeries of the no-wrap bounds must be rejected: a 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪\mathsf{ShiftQ8} row quantized at a too-large exponent with a wrapped minimality witness, rows whose 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪𝖲\mathsf{ShiftQ8S} or gate shift exceeds its bound, and left-shift rows built from the residues of Remark 6.3; so must a proof checked against model constants that differ from the prover’s, and tokens outside the vocabulary. A 𝖭𝗈𝗋𝗆𝖲𝖼𝖺𝗅𝖾\mathsf{NormScale} row normalized by a wrapped left shift is rejected, and the same proof verifies once the bound (16,[E<0]Σ)(16,[E<0]\,\Sigma) is removed from prover and verifier; for both signed normalizations, every wrapped left shift in a randomized search satisfies the field relation and is rejected by the input bound. For Qwen3, small models with QK-norm and with a mixture of 8 experts (4 per token) prove and verify end to end, with the prover’s witness checked against F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}; a head row’s requantization off by one entry, a router weight off by one, and a slot routed to an expert that was not selected are rejected. Every row clamp is exercised by models re-quantized so that some rows clamp and some sit exactly at the edge, and a flag forged on an edge row, which gives the same shift, is rejected. Two forgeries target wraps that the bounds of Section 6.6 exclude: QK-norm head rows claimed at exponent 22 through the unquartered minimality relation, which changes every generated token of the small model, and a router logit claimed saturated at kr=15k_{r}=15 (Section 6.6). Both are rejected, and both would be accepted with the unquartered relation or a router shift bound of 15. The device transcript and the graph-replayed prover are checked to produce byte-identical proofs to the host transcript and the plain prover. For the BLAKE3 circuit, a forged XOR byte with every arithmetic constraint repaired and a message word that differs between input rows and G rows are both rejected (Section 10).

12 Discussion

The price of exactness.

Sable proves the function a server runs, so the server must run F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}. F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} uses 8-bit matrix products with exact 32-bit accumulation, which integer tensor cores support, but its fused rounding steps, the 9-bit outputs of 𝖱𝗈𝖯𝖤𝟪\mathsf{RoPE8}, and the blocked P​VPV product need their own kernels. We wrote a serving engine for it that computes F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} bit for bit (checked token by token against the reference implementation): attention is an exact integer kernel in Triton that never forms the score matrix (products of 9-bit integers in fp16 with fp32 accumulation are exact while every partial sum stays below 2242^{24}, which the blocked P​VPV product guarantees), the integer element-wise work of each layer is compiled into fused kernels, and each decoding step is replayed as one CUDA graph. Table 17 compares it with BF16 and FP8 (W8A8, per-tensor scales) versions of the same model in SGLang [ZYX+24] on the same GPU.

At batch 1, decoding is bound by reading the weights, and F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}, with 8-bit weights, matches FP8 and is 30%30\% faster than BF16. At batch 32, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} decodes at 79%79\% of the FP8 rate: its exact attention and integer element-wise work cost more than FP8’s, and its 8-bit matrix products run on an older-generation cuBLASLt kernel (a tile configuration of the Ampere generation) than SGLang’s FP8 path. The largest gap is prefill, 2.72.7 times slower than FP8 at batch 32, because our engine prefills two sequences at a time with exact integer attention while SGLang batches them through tuned kernels. These are costs of any exact scheme: a proof about a floating-point computation would first have to fix the order of every reduction, which current kernels do not do [HT25].

Where the time goes, and what would reduce it.

Commitment, lookups and constraint terms account for almost all of the prover’s work. At long contexts, attention dominates, and the 1616K proof already uses 72 of the GPU’s 96 GiB. Every causal score entry costs one committed probability, one lookup and two constraint terms, and the probability must be committed because it is a lookup output. Sliding-window attention in most layers, as some current models use, would remove most of these entries. At short contexts, the prover is partly latency-bound; batching the many small sumchecks of a layer into fewer, larger ones, and moving the remaining host-side claim arithmetic to the GPU, are the next steps there. Univariate skip for the first round [Gru24] would save an estimated 2%2\% to 4%4\%.

Soundness parameters.

The tightest terms of Table 2 are the queries (103.4103.4 bits, of which 30 are proof of work) and the lookups (103.9103.9 bits, of which 11 are proof of work). That margin is what a composition with up to four recursive layers needs to stay above 100 bits overall. The lookup term depends on drawing one coefficient per tuple coordinate: with the powers of a single challenge, which is a common choice, tuples of arity seven would lose log2⁡6≈2.6\log_{2}6\approx 2.6 bits (Lemma 8.1) and the term would drop to 101.3101.3 bits. Likewise, an exact left shift in a 31-bit field needs a bound on its input as well as on its output (Remark 6.3).

Proof size and recursion.

A main proof of 106 to 477 MiB suits an auditor; returning one with every response is impractical. Reducing it has so far reduced the recursion’s input as well: the verifier’s hashing fell by 4.2×4.2\times. The remaining verifier work is dominated by GKR challenges and leaf hashing; fewer GKR rounds (wider fraction trees, or fewer separate trees per domain) and larger work units would reduce both. Our BLAKE3 circuit is within 30%30\% of the cell count assumed by the design, but the commitment of its trace is not yet measured, and an algebraic hash would make the recursion several times cheaper at the cost of a further assumption.

Zero knowledge.

The main proof reveals evaluations of the trace and is meant for the requesting client. Multi-tenant proofs, closed weights that must stay secret, and publication of proofs all need zero knowledge; without it, about 1.9×1041.9\times 10^{4} proofs reveal the weights (Section 4), and a batch reveals its prompts to every verifier of the batch. For multilinear arguments this requires hiding commitments (random symbols in every column, salted leaves), masked sumcheck and GKR messages in the style of [CFS17, XZZ+19], and lookup roots sent only per chunk. Each piece is standard; their combination with a streamed, chunked prover needs its own analysis.

Accuracy.

F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}’s perplexity is 8.3%8.3\% above BF16’s, against 0.7%0.7\% for FP8. Wider queries and keys would recover about a third of the gap at an estimated 30 to 68% more proving time (Section 11.8); we have not located the rest. On Qwen3, a better split of the existing score precision between queries and keys removed about a quarter to a half of the gap at no proving cost, which suggests that calibration still has room before formats must widen; finding integer formats that close the gap at a small proving cost is the main open question for F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}}. Task benchmarks deserve the same scrutiny as perplexity: on Qwen3 a few nats of logit error matter more on MMLU than on Qwen2.5 because the model’s own margins are smaller, and on GSM8K most of the loss of Qwen3-32B came from a change of answer style.

Generality.

Besides Qwen2.5-32B, we evaluated two Qwen3 models: a dense one with QK-norm and a mixture of experts with 128 experts per layer (Section 5.6). Both reuse the protocol and add gadgets: QK-norm is the existing requantization and normalization applied per head row, and the experts are selected by a threshold argument and a dynamic multiset and multiplied by gathered sumchecks (Section 6.6). Other attention variants change the tile list. Other architectures change the gadget composition and keep the protocol.

13 Conclusion

Sable shows that bit-exact proofs of production-size language model inference are feasible on one GPU. The full 64-layer Qwen2.5-32B is proven in 92.5 seconds for 4,096 tokens and in under seven minutes for 16,384 tokens, 41 to 50 times the time of the inference it attests and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. The same prover handles QK-norm and a mixture of experts: it proves 4,096 tokens of Qwen3-32B in 121.8 seconds and of Qwen3-30B-A3B, whose tokens each use 8 of 128 experts per layer, in 84.7 seconds, and on both models F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} stays within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. Three ingredients make this possible. An integer function fixes every rounding decision of the model. A constraint system over a 31-bit field never wraps, and its chunked lookups remain sound beyond pp lookups. A streamed prover recomputes the witness where it would otherwise store it, and replays identical layers as GPU graphs. The same proof system proves BLAKE3 compressions at a few microseconds each, which is the basis for compressing the main proof recursively. Served by an engine that computes it exactly, F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} decodes as fast as FP8 at batch 1 and at 79%79\% of its rate at batch 32. The remaining costs are a proof that takes about 50 times the inference it attests, an integer function that loses accuracy against BF16, and, until the recursive layers with zero knowledge exist, a proof suited to auditors of open-weight models. The next steps are those layers, a verifier compiled as a whole, and integer formats that recover the lost accuracy.

Lemma A.1 (Row maximum).

Suppose the gather set of a key-value group sums to zero as a rational function, the range lookups m−jm∗∈[0,224)m-j^{\ast}_{m}\in[0,2^{24}) and jm∗−sm∈[0,224)j^{\ast}_{m}-s_{m}\in[0,2^{24}) hold with sms_{m} the first position of mm’s sequence, Mm=∑cQ^m​c​Km​cgM_{m}=\sum_{c}\hat{Q}_{mc}K^{g}_{mc}, and (𝖤𝖷𝖯,xm​j,Pm​j)∈𝒯(\mathsf{EXP},x_{mj},P_{mj})\in\mathcal{T} for every kept entry. Then Mm=maxsm≤j≤m⁡accm​jM_{m}=\max_{s_{m}\leq j\leq m}\mathrm{acc}_{mj} and Pm​j=τexp​(Mm−accm​j)P_{mj}=\tau_{\exp}(M_{m}-\mathrm{acc}_{mj}) for every valid jj.

Proof.

The gather set has fewer than pp reads, so by Lemma 3.2 every read tuple (jm∗,c,Km​cg)(j^{\ast}_{m},c,K^{g}_{mc}) equals a table-side tuple (j,c,K^j​c)(j,c,\hat{K}_{jc}). The range lookups, over integers below 2242^{24}, give sm≤jm∗≤ms_{m}\leq j^{\ast}_{m}\leq m, so jm∗j^{\ast}_{m} is a valid key. For every valid jj, the softmax lookup has input Mm−accm​jM_{m}-\mathrm{acc}_{mj} (with νm​j=1\nu_{mj}=1 on diagonal tiles); both scores are integers below 2222^{22} in absolute value, so the field value Mm−accm​jM_{m}-\mathrm{acc}_{mj} lies in the table’s domain [0,223)[0,2^{23}) only if the integer difference does. Hence Mm≥accm​jM_{m}\geq\mathrm{acc}_{mj} for every valid jj, with equality at jm∗j^{\ast}_{m}. The table has one row per input, so Pm​jP_{mj} is its output. ∎

A.7 Determinism of F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} (Lemma 5.1)

F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is a fixed composition of the operations of Section 5.2, each of which is a function of its inputs. The ranges claimed for intermediate values follow from the same bounds as Table 18: 𝖱𝖾𝗊𝗎𝖺𝗇𝗍𝟪\mathsf{Requant8} and 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪\mathsf{ShiftQ8} never clip, by the half-open fitting interval; 𝖲𝗁𝗂𝖿𝗍𝖰𝟪𝖲\mathsf{ShiftQ8S} clips by definition; the softmax probabilities are at most 2102^{10}, so Dm≤210​SD_{m}\leq 2^{10}S and each P​VPV block is below 2292^{29}; the rounded blocks sum to less than 2232^{23} because km≥Emk_{m}\geq E_{m} and Dm<2Em+16D_{m}<2^{E_{m}+16}; and 𝖲𝖺𝗍𝖠𝖽𝖽\mathsf{SatAdd} returns a value in AA. The quantities whose range F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} requires without implying it (the SiLU input |c|≤214|c|\leq 2^{14}, the shift ranges, and inputs of left shifts with |2−k​acc|≤223|2^{-k}\mathrm{acc}|\leq 2^{23}) are checked by the honest prover, which aborts if one fails; for such inputs F𝖮F_{\mathsf{O}} is undefined. Section 11.9 measures how often this happens. ∎
